nt tDUCATED ILAIDES, • blie's a dainty little maiden, With artistic graces laden, quite aware of her attractions, and rejoicing in tar Was ; She parades, with ostentation, All her college education, With a reminiscent flavouring of culture and ealgtees.

With suggestions by the legion She can scale the airy region 'Where the transcedental fantasies in gay diserder boat, With langour rare and queenly She can voyage most serenely MairOUgh the hazy sublimation of the misty and remota.

Size cati:ead the rocky pages Of the geologic ages, 'When the mighty megathenum was etteping in the lair, With features bright and smiting She is often most beguiling Whseeclieval narratives of knight and" ladye fair."

She is often entertaining When most learnedly.exp!aining Row the philosophic systems in a measure disagree; She is posted in quadratics And the higher matheinatics, Andean ask for the butter in the language of" ?tree."

She's uneducated daisy, And cenki run a fellow crazy With a stock of information too enormous to rehearse. She brought away from college Such immeasurable knowledge Of the corroletive members cf the wizzing universe. Still, I hope this gentle maiden. ARMAGEDDON. A WAR ISOKO OF THLIZ FIITTIRIL ltrarChing down to Armageddon— Brothers, stout and strong! Let us cheer the way we tread on With a soldier's song! Faint we by the weary road, Or fall we in the rout, _ Dirge or Paean, Death or Triumph I-- Let the song ring out! .1 "Mt We are they who scorn the scorners Love the levers—hate None within the world's four corners— All must share one fate; We are they whose common banner Bears no badge or sign, Save the light which dyes it white— The Hope that makes it shine. We are they whose bugle rings, ;

That all the wars may cease; We are they will pay the Kings Their cruel price for Peace; We are they whose steadfast watchword: fs what Christ did teach,— 'Each man for his Brother first— And Heaven, then, for each." We are they who will not falter— Many swords or few— Till we make this Earth the altar Of a worship new; We are they who will not take From palace, priest, or code, A meaner Law than" Brotherhood"—
A lower Lord than GOD. Marching down the Armageddon— Brothers, stout and strong! Ask not why the way we tread on: Is so rough and long ! God will tell us when our spirits

Grow to grasp His plan! Lit us do our part to-day-- And help Him, helping Man!: Shall we even curse the madness, ' • Which for "ends of State," Dooms us to the long, long sadness, Of this human hate? Let us slay in perfect pity, Those that must not live; Vanquish, and forgive our foes— Or fall,—and still forgive! We are those whose unpaid legions, In free ranks arrayed, Massacred in many regions— sever once were stayed; We are they Whose torn battalions— Trained to bleed, not fly! Make our agonies a triumph— Conquer, while we die. Therefore, down the Armageddon— Brothers, bold and strong; Cheer the glorious way we tread on - With this soldier's song! Let the armies of the old Flags March in silent dread! Death and Life are one to us, Who fight for Quick and Dead! EDWIN ARNOLD,

Never court inquiry when you are wedded to your own opinions. It's a jealous wife that won't allow her husband to embrace a fair opportunity, "What one girl did !" is the title of a new story. She doubtless did the same as all other girls do—, jumped upon a table and frightened a poor little mouse to death. A little fellow, looking rather squeamish, went into a Scotch grocery store, and, with a very doleful look, asked for a pennyworth of salts. During the operation of the weighing the article he said to the grocer, "Diana gie's full weight, for it's me that has to tak' them." One day a Fife miner was descending the pit when the wire rope broke, and he was precipitated to the bottom, a depth of fourteen fathoms. At once the men who happened to be working near the pit bottom rushed to the spot, crying, "Oh, there's a man killed !" but much to their surprise and relief the supposed corpse called out, although unable to stir, "Na, na, he's no' deid yet. Dae you think I never gaeddoon a pit afore?" Tem PAINTED AND THE KlNS.—Richard Wilson, the first great English painter of landscape, and whose works nowadays fetch high prices, spent most of his life in much distress. On one occasion, driven by poverty, he asked a painter of historical subjects—James Barry, RA.—whether he knew anybody insane enough to em- ploy a landscape painter, for if he did he begged that he might be recommended, as he had actually no work. It IS said that Wilson painted a view of Sion House for George the Third, and asked sixty guineas for it. Lord Bute remonstrated with him about the price, saying that it was to high. The unhappy artist retinted in- dignantly that if the King could not pay the sum all at once, he might pay it in instalments.—Litae Folks Diaga- rine, TILE FANS OF ARBAN.—Af ter the land is natio nalised, and the Duke sent to the rightabout, we shall have a big hotel up here, with a patent lift, seven-o'clock table el*hote, and a Church of England chaplain. Meantime it remains a majestic solitude, where, except for the hoarse croak of the raven or the pitiful wail of the whaup, the silence is seldom broken. High up in the ether a peregrine watches us with jealous eyes; a pack of grouse sweep round the boulders and duck into the valley at our feet; these and such as these are the only natives visible. The inevitable Mr. Cook is still conspicuous by his absence. Fancy to yourself a prolonged battlement, with a square tower at intervals of a mile or so, and you obtain a very fair idea of the great central range from Sui Ferghus to Ben Noosh. The massive wall is never less than two thousand feet in height. The highest of these towers is close upon three thousand. This is "Cyclopean archi- tecture indeed, and in all Scotland, nay in all Europe, You will hardly anywhere match these gigantic slabs, piled one upon the other by cunningest masonry into the air ! —" Shirley," in " Good Words." DITIDIVG ma Sroms.—President Cleveland's sayings have a striking resemblance to some of Mr. Lincoln's. Indeed, People are tracing wherein the two resemble each other. For instance, the other clay half a dozen good and true Democrats from a Western State went to the White House to see the President about certain offices they had come for. There was perfect agreement among themselves, and all they wanted was to have Mr. Cleveland agree with them. Of his doing so-they had little doubt when he had heard them state their ease. They were admitted, and a hearty handskaking followed. Then the spokesman of the party spoke up. "You see," said he "we're all Democrats, hard workers for the Party, and have concluded that these offices would be about the fair thing. We're all agreed about the busi- ness, and would like to have it done up right soOn." Mr. Cleveland listened attentively as they all spoke round. When they had done so he spoke. "Are the men in the offices not of good character?" They all said they were, and added—" But they are Republicans and we're Democrats. We think turn-about would be the fair thing." "Are you prepared to charge them with anything wrong in office ? Do they administer the offices satisfactorily ?" They said they had 'nothing to charge against them, only they were Republicans. "You see," said one, perceiving where the thing was drifting, "we all worked hard for the party last fall, and our dis- trict gave a larger majority than ever. We thought the offices would go with the election, and so we've come for them." "When will the term of the incumbents expire ?" asked the President. They all spoke up—" Two rare "Two years," repeated the President, musingly, imme- diately adding—" Come and see me then I"

Che Raswito CART HORSRS.—We take the following extract from Mr. F. Street's recent lecture before the Institute of Agriculture :—" Let us start with a mare in foal, say at Michaelmas. It will be far better for the mare to be turned in a cool yard at night, during the winter months, than to be kept in a warm stable. A liberal diet of oats, bran, and hay is necessary; by no means give mangolds, it makes them shoot the coat too early in the following spring. If mares foal in early spring, or at any later period, I hold it essential for the well being of the offspring that the mare should be turned on pasture for at least three weeks before foal- ine, to get used to the change from dry food; foals will stand what exposure the dam has been accustomed to. How often does one hear of the loss of foals from eold, inflammation, or diarrheea through mares being turned out on succulent pasture for the first time after foaling. Mares kept for breeding purposes only—not required to work—are better to have dry food given on pasture dur- ing winter. For a time after foaling mares should have oats given them morning and evening, then grass alone will be sufficient. I like for foals, when a month or five weeks old, to be shut away from their dams for an hour or two each day to be taught to eat dry food, as bran and grittled oats. Before weaning the foals can-be separated from the mares longer at a time, and when taken away entirely will not lose flesh to the same ex- tent as is often the case when suddenly taken from their mothers and weaned. I strongly recommend, where practicable, the advisability a young animals being raised on pasture instead of in loose boxes or warm yards. Ido not, however, wish to be misunderstood and supposed to advocate this treatment in all cases— as in the case of backward or delicate foals. The advan- tage of having hedges for shelter or suitable climate will regulate this. Ido not even care for a hovel for ..shelter, for, however severe the weather, in ninety- nine times out of a hundred you will find the foals in the open. I have never known a case of injury from eating frosted grass. By this treatment the growth of bone, mesele, and hair will be encouraged, the constitution strengthened, the elasticity of action retained, whilst -the danger of getting over on their joints, or flying at the hocks is reduced to a minimum. Foals require good and suitable dry food during the winter months. At no .other period of life will they so well repay the outlay'. Size will never afterwards be obtained, unless the foals are well grown when young. I may add I practice the above-named plan. bline of my earliest foals have never been under shelter other than hedges this winter, whilst the very late foals lie in a cool yard at nigin„.and run on a pasture in the day-time. During the summer months dry food can be omitted, grass alone being sufficient. It will be advantageous to supplement grass by gi.ring dry food during the second or any succeeding winter. Some may remark that this plan may be all very well for or- dinary purpeses, but will it answer for those animals intended for •exhibition purposes ? I will remark that at the first shows in Loudon the practice was to being yearlings into the ring as if they had come out of IA baud-box, but the aim for the last year or two has been to retain the wiuter coat. Judges do not favour an ac- cumulation of fat-in some young animals, but require bone and muscle wills activity. To prove that animals so treated can not only be exhibited successfully, but also disposed of remuneratively, I have only to point out to you that the Elsetsham stud have been raised en- tirely on this principle of training. The ;remarks I heard when attending this wonderful sale were—when forty animals averaged over £172 each—' they were the soundest lot of animals ever brought into a sale ring.' Mr. Gilbey assured me not one of the fillies had been housed for more than a few days previous to the sale."

amen. A BIRD-KILLING TRlSR.—There is In New Zealand a tree which proves fatal to birds in an altogether singular way. The seed vessels give off a sticky fluid, and many a fly finds itself imprisoned in the gummy stuff. These flies, in turn, attract small birde,and they also get so covered with the fluid that they are unable to flutter. The fruit, too, is an object of desire, and birds become, as it were, glued to the ripe clusters which they pro- pesed to eat. The wee birds cannot escape without help, and so they lie there, a prey to ether animals. A black cat took up its home near °lmo f these trees for the purpose of dining on the poor birds, and pussy herself had to obtain aid every now and then in order to remove the sticky pods that gotinto her fur.---Litt/s Folks' Maga- zine. A DECOY ron Cnows.—On the Continent, hunters adopt a curious plan for attracting the crows which they wish to destroy. These birds attack all owls during the day, as they know that the bright sunlight dazzles them ' to such an extent as to render them incapable of de- fending themselves. So what does the bunter do? He claim an owl to a post furnished witla a small platform upon which it can sit, and employs it as a decoy. Near this post a hut is put up, the side next the post having several loopholes through which the gun-barrels can be pushed. A chain or rope, working on pulleys, extends from the platform to the hut, so that by pulling the chain the platform on which the owl rests can be moved up and down, and the bird made to flutter its wings, and thus attract the attention of its foes. They soon sur- round the decoy owl in goodly numbers, and begin to pester the poor bird unmercifully. Its persecution, however, does not last long, for the hurcter is all the while taking a leisurely aim, and when be fires a great many birds are slain. These "crow-huts," as they are styled, are generally erected close to a large tree, as some birds of prey usually take a short rest before as- saulting the owl. This decoy may be successful with the German crows, but I am sure the rooks at home here would soon find out what it meant. This whole- sale destruction of birds may be necessary in localities where they are specially mischievous, but, on •other grounds, it seems quite a mockery to call this slaughter eport.—Little Folks Magazine. "Well, now we've got on to musical stories;"-said An ex-manager, "there occurs to my mind an amusing in- cident that occurred in the orchestra during my man- agement of the Walnut-street"Theatre years ago. Our musicians, like those of most places of amusement, were allowed to send substitutes when they could get a good outside engagement for a night or so. At the time of which I speak we had two trombones, and were playing An overture in which there was a beautiful duet 'for 'those two instruments. Our first trombone player hav- ing accepted an engagement to play for a ball, found it. impossible to obtain a substitute, and, as a last resort, determined to employ-in-that capacity a young friend of his who couldn't play a note. All you have to do,' mid. the trombone wrestler, is to watch what the other trembone player does, and imitate his movements. As there are two trombones, -the silence of one will never .be noticed.' Thus instructed, the youth came to the theatre and took his plaee in the orchestra with muck, trepidation. The overture progressed smoothly to the duo for the trombones. The other instruments ceased. The leader beat time for the duet with his bow, and so accustomed had his ears become he the familiar sounds that he did not notice their absence for several seconds. Then he turned to see what the silesee meant, and be- held the twA trombone players with their hands frantic- ally grasping their instruments, their Cheeks distended, and their eyes Axed upon each other with an expression of the wildest agony and despair. The fact was that the second trombone player had also sent as a substitute a young man 971}1i) couldn't play, and had also instructed bin' to watch and imitate the other wind-jaminer." BismAncies MARESAGF..—One of the neighbours with whom he lived upon terms of intimacy was Moritz von Blankenburg, and in his house he made the aequaint- ance of Johanna von Putkammer, which, during a journey which the two made in company with their common friends, ripened to a deep and lasting affection. The young lady's parents were very quiet and deeply religious persons, and when the "mad Lord of Kniephof" wrote to ask their daughter's hand, and she confessed that she had given him her heart, their consternation was great. The father confessed that "he felt as if he had been struck on the head with an axe ;" but he did not feel justified in opposing the wishes of the young people. The mother was more obdurate and it was only when Bismarck appeared to plead his own cause that she granted her consent, But having yielded, she did so frankly and without reserve. She wel- comed her future son-in-law not only to her home, but to her heart; and he proved himself thoroughly worthy of her confidence. He became a real member of the family, and the first serious difference which he had with the parents of his wife was also the last. The marriage was celebrated on the 28th Ju1y,1847. To understand the effect which this union had on the whole character of the future statesman, it is necessary to remember several things. He was at this time deeply disgusted with his past life. He had tried excess and found it a weariness, he was tired of the monotony of dissipa- tion. He had been cast hither and thither by the waves of chance and humour, and was fully pursuaded that the end of all this is vanity. While young in body and in mind, and dimly conscious that he possessed unusual powers he could find no ideal, no aim, and no ambition that fired and satisfied his imagination. With religion in the true sense of the word he had never been brought into contact until he wooed her in his bride. In his youth, two spiritual influences had been predominant in P,russia— the deism of Voltaire slightly modified by that of Leasing, and the mysticism of the Romantic School which was verging more and more clearly into Roman Catholicism. From the latter tendency his father's house had been almost completely free, and what he saw of it in later years was not calculated to attract the keen-eyed, hard- headed, and open-hearted youth. Without for a moment calling the sincerity of the Romantic loaders into ques- tion, it must be admitted that for most of them Catholi- cism was a matter of taste and the imagination rather than of the head, the heart, or the conscience. It is in this that they differ so widely from our English converts of later days. The Roman Church, as they understood it, made life look pretty; so they chose it. Bismarck was seeking for realities, not for dreams. Had he come under the influence of a man like Cardinal Newman, th whom every dogma is not only a truth but a key to the whole ,problem of human existence, the case might have been different, as it was, the mediaeval legends over which his contemporaries were poring interested him rather less than the mythology of Greece and Rome., But in his wife and her family he was brought face to face with a new power. Here were men and women, leading not only blameless but active and useful lives, who had as strong a hold on the external reality of the world as any one, and who yet were moved by motives that were not of this world, but constantly felt they were in the presence of a judge, a father, and a friend. In such a conviction he, too, might find a motive and an aim. Like Goethe, he had sought consolation and strength in the ethics of Spinoza; but, unlike the great poet, he had not succeeded in finding them there. The thought of a personal loyalty to a personal God, on the other hand, appealed to the deepest impulses of his nature; and the home into which he, the wild wanderer, had been re- mitred, with hesitation at first, it is true, but then in _perfect affection and confidence, was so calm and quiet That it seemed as if the peace that passeth understand- ing brooded over it, as indeed it did. Bismarck became deeply imbued with his wife's religious convictions, and he found in them the motive power that had hitherto been wanting in his life. This was the turning point; from henceforth he had a purpose that filled and satis- fied his whole being—to do his duty before a living God. Doubtless, like all of us, he has fallen short of his ideal, and still more undoubtedly, in the opinion of most, he has mistaken his duty; but always there has been a power within him which enabled him to despise the praise of men, and to appeal to a higher standard than the phrase or the fashion of the hour.—Temple Bar. The Times says :—The most interesting feature in the debate on ' Monday was Mr. Gladstone's incidental suggestion, in a moment of irritation, provoked by some unseemly interruptions, that his retirement from the House of Commune was not far distant. To the minds of many who heard him speak this utterance of the Prime Minister apparently conveyed the impression that at the close of the present session he intended to retire from public life, and neither retain tbe leadership of the Liberal party nor seek to be elected to a reformed House of Com- mons. But the remark—a criite natural one in the mouth of a statesman in his 76 h year—does not necessarily Lear so precise a meaning, and indeed for many years past Mr. Gladstone has from time to time made ate of similar lan- guage without any immediate result. Tan BLUE IidEBON UOTEL TEMPERANCE MOVEMENT. —The annual meeting ou behalf of this movement took place in Exeter Hall on Monday night under the presi- dency of Mr. W. 1. Palmer, J.P., of Reading, the president, There was a large audience.—The report stated that the mission movement had resulted in a large increase to the ranks of individual workers. Public-house visitation had been carried on, and 2.920 pledges had been taken at the summer processions on Saturday afternoons. A new poc- ket pledge book had been published, the use of which had resulted in 23,700 p'edges. Mr. Noble bad conducted ex- tended missions in many provincial towns. The exp ndi• ture had been £1,362 7s, and the receipts £1,244. The chairman said " tiospei Temperance" meant a direct ap- peal to the churches of this land to help them in their work, and he wanted 'Clem to realise their duties in this respect. The following resolution was adopted :—" That this meet- ieg expresses its satisfaction that the Government have re- solved not to impose any increased taxation upon the neces- saries of life, and trusts that the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer will retain his Budget proposal intact, as far as the taxes on spirits Awl beer see concerned."

lie SIIFFOLL-Of crossing a stile at evening into a cer- tain favourite high field open to the west, whence the spirit could go voyaging among the happy archipelagoes of the sunset sky, while dusk and mist were filling the valley at my feet. Of the enchantment of winter frosts, with icicles fringing the eaves, and the garden trees glittering all transfigured in the tingling air. Or again of Sunday afternoons at church in summer, where through the open side-door the familiar landscape of clustered cottages and basking meadows and wooded slopes lay framed and glowing in the quiet sunshine, while the cawing of the rooks and the crooning of the wood-pigeons floated in from the treetops to temper the discord of our rustic psalmody. Dozens of such detailed images will rise up at chance moments before me, and there are no glories of the world that I have ever seen— no purple-flowered and torrent-cloven valley over which the majesty of Monte Rosa hangs aureoled at sunset—. not the view from above Athens, over the blue of the Saronic gulf, to /Egina and the fair procession of the Argive hills—not the hourly change of gloom and glory over the flashing straits and proud-peaked mountain- islands of the Hebrides—there is not one of these scenes which, fully as at the time I may have felt-its power, I can yet honestly and in truth recall as vividly, or with such a stirring of the spirit, as those simple and bounded prospects of my Suffolk home.—Sidney Colein, in the , "Magazine of Art."

THE MANAGEMENT OF POULT ItY• DISEASES OF Tile RESPIRATORY ORGANS. One of the results of bad housing, or want of ventilation In houses is that diseases affectiag the respiratory organs are induced, and we thus find such complaints as catarrh, bronchitis, incipient roup, and even consumption. The use of badly built houses, in which the birds are exposed to draughts or damp, or of badly ventilated houses, in which the inmates live in a foul, close atmosphere, and are thus in a fit state to be attacked by cold when they go out into the open air, are both equally inducive to respiratory diseases. The form these diseases takes is of tendecided by the state of body in the first place, except in oontagious diseases, when the contagion decides the matter. As in all forms of disease the important point is to take it in time, we shall endeavour to describe the ,symptoms fully, so as to give as far as possible an indi- cation of the complaint. It is, however, always to be remembered that the treatment of dumb animals is more difficult than that of human beings. They cannot describe their feelings, and these have more or less to be guessed at. As the same apparent symptom may be resultant from two or three causes, mistakes are often made but this is our misfortune rather than our fault. Consttrit outlook should be observed, and an attendant who takes any interest in the fowls can soon discern when anything is wrong, for the first thing noted is generally the huddling up of the fowls in a corner. When this is seen it should be separated from the rest, and put in some warm pen, whore the developments can be easily noted, and where it will be prevented from infecting others should the disease be proved infectious or contagious. Healthy fowls often ill-use a sick one, and for this reason such an one should be removed. CATARRH.—One of the commonest diseases is cold in the head, or catarrh, which in some cases developes until it resembles influenza. This is the result of damp or exposure, and may be induced, as in the human subject, by an unexpected change in the weather. Generally the first symptoms are a ruffling of the feathers as if the bird felt cold, and then sneezing and running at the nos- trils. If this be not dealt with the eyes begin to swell, and unless the treatment succeeds the nostrils will be- erne stepped up with mucous, and the eyes almost, if not entirely, closed. In this latter stage the complaint is very infectious, and even if taken early it is often difficult to prevent it affecting an entire yard. During the laying season this is serious, as often the eggs are stopped, and it is especially troublesome when a hen with a brood of chickens becomes affected. Warmth is most essential to overcome catarrh. If so kept there need be little trouble in conquering it during the early stages. Soft food, of a nourishing nature, should be given, and this may be sprinkled with pepper or ginger. If taken at the first nothing can be better as medicine than camphor (pilules are the easiest to administer), but later on doses of homceopathic tincture of aconite are to be preferred. If the discharge from the nostrils becomes very profuse, we should recommend homceopathic tinc- ture of arsenicum. Spratt's Patent have a roup paste which is highly recommended for the later stages of this complaint. In addition to what is given in the form of medicine the nostrils and eyes of the bird should be washed twice a day with warm water, to which about one-sixth of vinegar has been added. We have also heard that holding tho fowl's head over steam made by pouring boiling water upon a few hops is most useful, but care has to be taken that further cold does not result BRONCHITIS.—In cases where there is an inherent weakness in the lungs or chest, cold often develops into bronchitis, but we have very seldom found it take this form except there has been very great neglect) unless there is such weakness. Hence the vast importance of breeding from sound, healthy stock, and we should strongly urge all who have had a bird attacked by bron- chitis not to breed from it. Even though cured, it will transmit a taint to its progeny. Much of the disease found amongst domestic poultry is due to the use of stock fowls which are affected in this way. Bronchitis is generally indicated by a rattle in the throat and a i cough. If the breathing s hard, there will be rapid respiration noticed. Usually cold in the head is not present, and the skin is dry and hot. There is dulness, and in the majority of cases loss of appetite. If not stopped, all.these symptoms increase, until the breathing can be heard some distance away. Medicine is compara- tively of little avail with bronchitis. It may aid a cure, but will not without proper external measures are used. Warmth, moist warmth, is required, for dry air aggra- vates the disease. Steaming the apartment or pen in which the fowl is placed is most useful, and the water should be medicated with hops, poppy-heads, or a few drops of carbolic acid. Warm, soft food must be given, and a little aromatic compound mixed with this. To the drinking water may be added five drops of nitric acid, sweetened with sugar. A remedy has been intro- duced of late by Messrs. Thos. Christy and Co., of Lon- don, which is said to be a wonderful cure for bronchitis and coughs. It is called euphorbia, pilulifora, and is a vegetable remedy. We have not had an opportunity of trying it ourselves, but those who have used it speak of it very highly. Sometimes there is a form of laboured breathing which is ,more like asthma than bronchitis, as it is unaccompanied by any cough. It is less dangerous, and partakes muse of a chronic nature. For it the euphorbia pilulifere should be employed. SEASONABLE HINTS. Those who have chickens must remember that as the birds get old they will require more room and more air. This is especially the case with those that are reared in Artificial Mothers; but eYen with such as are under hens they need to be treated differently than at an earlier period of the year. Coops are often made too little, and both hen and chickens are erowded therein. This, with the expanding size of the latter, is a mistake. If there are spare houses about, and sow that the breeding sea- son is over, several lots of hees can be put together, so as to make some houses at liberty. It is a good plan to give a hen and brood one of these houses. We recently saw a capital method described to induce chickens to settle in a large house without the hen. It was to nail a couple of strips of wood over the entrance to the house, so that the hen was unable to get out but the chickens could. In a day or two she was taken away, and they renlained contented in their new home.

A Birmingham man made a bet that he could invent a question to which fifty people would all give the same answer. He won the bet. The question was—" Have you heard that Smith has committed suicide ?" The answer in each case was—" What Smith?"

Knowles, situate on Me banks of the river Anker, at Nuneaton, were destroyed by lire, 1.000 quarters of wheat have been destroyed or spoiled, as well as 1,500 sacks of Hour and immense quantities of sharps, barley, barley meal, bran, &a. The damage is estimated at over £60,000. Veers Alwyn, MEAT.—Overdone beef or mutton is quite as indigestible as hard-boiled eggs; it should be welt cooked to be healthful, but rather inclining to be underdone. Roasting retains the juices of ~the meat; boiling does not, but the liquor in which meat has been boiled may be used as soup. Made dishes are not so whole- some or easily digested as joints, and if much flavouring or rich sauces be used they are bad indeed for the dyspep- tic. Veal does not suit the dyspeptic well. Tho fat of beef is digestible, that of mutton less so, and that of game is apt to disagree. Much of the flavour of meat , lies in the fat immediately beneath the skin. Mils. S. A. div.head: UR. BRADLAUGH, M.P., AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: UR. BRADLAUGH, M.P., AT WAR- RINGTON.

On Saturday evening Mr. C. Bradlangh, M.P., addressed a meeting in the Co-operative Hall, Warrington, on" Our position in Egypt and the Soudan; the blunder of 1875 and the crime since." The chair was occupied by Mr. H. Whitham, and there was a good attendance.

The CHAIRMAN said he Might just be allowed to say a few words. It would be quite within the memory of most of them, or at least of those who took an active part in poli- tics, that during the past winter they had had in Warring- ton two series of political lectures, one series got up by the Liberal party, and the other by the Conservative party. The Liberals had had for their object the educating of the people generally, irrespective of party ; they had tried to sketch out what was their work in the future, and also to illustrate that work by the •work they had done in the past. The Conservative party had had a series of meetings, but they had been held at what they termed ward or business meetings-- meetings of '',/a setni-private character, at which when advanced Liberals or Radicals wished to attend, the Conservatives kindly told them they were not wanted. (Hear, hear.) lie remembered that at one of their meetings the subject,was "Radicalism and Ruin," as it the two terms were synonymous. (Laughter.) A few friends had desired to hear a little bit of the subject, but they were refused ad- mittance. (Hear, hear.) They would notice that through- out the country the two political parties used a large amount of recriminatory language. Tim Liberals when in office say that all their miechances are in consequence of what the Conservatives did when they were in office, and the Conservatives, on their part, say that the Liberals bring about all their misfortunes by their own blundering. But it se happened that there was growing up in the country another party, outside the Liberal and Conservative parties, and this party is termed the Radical party, and being out- side the other two parties it was able to look on and judge. (Hear, hear.) They would no doubt have noticed that the lecture of that evening was on " Our position in Egypt and the Seedan ; the blunder of 1875 and the crime since," and that implied that while the Conservatives were not likely to be spared that evening, neither were the Liberals likely to be spared. The lecturer would point out that neither party was in a right position; they had both been guilty of doing wrong. (Hear, hear.) In introducing Mr. Bradlaugh he mentioned that at the end of the lecture questions might be asked and a reasonable amount ef discussion allowed. In any part he (the chairman) had taken in political matters ,he had always recognised one thing, and that was that the political platform should be held sacred, that no one should interfere with those that occupied it, but that all should have a right to question the lecturer or speaker so long as it was done decently. (Applause.) MR. BRantAnorr, who was received with loud applause, said that his allegation was that all the mischief which was • now happening in Egypt and the Soudan, misehief which
mrts far lrom being finished yet, and which slam _1875 had

cost them in bard-cash and In guaranteed responsibilities at least £25,000,000, and was likely to cost them a great deal more, originated in the policy of foreign aggrandisement of the Tory Government during the time it was in office, and that in Egypt especially it originated with the purchase of the Suez Canal shares in 1875, which was one phase of a policy which had its outcome in the search tor a "scientific frontier" on the north-west of India and in the interference in Zululand. In speaking to them on that subject he lied at least one advantage over most politicians, and that was that what he should say about Egypt that night was precisely what he said in the wiater of 1875 6. He then stood al- most alone, with the exception that in the months of January and February Mr. Gladstone.—(applause)—in the House of Commons said some of the things inside that he (Mr. Bradlaugh) was saying outside. There was no support given by the Liberal party at that time . to the position. 'There was a notion which prevailed amongst Liberals as I well as amongst Conservatives that two good things were done at any rate, one of which was that great influence was got for us in Egypt, and the next was that a very satisfac- tory and profitable bargain had been made by the purchase ot the Suez Canal shares. The case with regard to the shares had been put very strongly hy Mr. Ashmead Bart- lett. (" Oh, eh," and laughter.) He did not think they ought to treat that gentleman with disdain as he possessed rather more than the average intelligence of a Conservative. (Laughter.) Mr. Bertlett said that it was Lord Bea.conaileld whip made British influence paramount in Egypt, and made for this country a splendid purchase of a large interest in the Suez Canal, the shares being now worth three times the SUM which he gave for, them, England having paid for them about .£4,000,000, and they were now worth at least £1.2,600i000. There was not a syllable of that true, and he would prove it to them. In 1875 Ismael, the then Viceroy of Egypt owned a large number of shares, some of which were dividend-paying shares and some of them paying no dividend. Those that paid no dividena we bought. (Laugh- ter.) Until 1894 they neither pay dividend nor do they give any right of vote or speech at any one of the share- holders' meetings. (Hear, hear.) All the shares then bought did not qualify ons directoe, and when he wanted to appoint directors of the Siws Canal, air. Disraeli had to buy shares in the open market out of the British taxpayers' pocket. In order to deceive the English public a guarantee was taken from Ismael that five per cent, should be paid on the purchase money, but that guarantee was not worth the paper it was written upon, (Hear, hear.) At that time a Conservative editor in this district said that he (hr. Brad- laugh) dealt with the character of a great prince in a way that reflected upon him—the editor put in one or two ad- jectives and adverbs which he would not try to remember out of regard for his own feelings—(laughter)—but the truth was that Ismael was insolvent—though this Warring- ton editor did not know it—and as a proof that he was inselvent he suspended payment a little later on. (Laughter, aid hear, hear.) The Government of that day either knew that Ismael could not keep the bargain they entered into with him, or they did not know. If they did know they were deceiving the English public, and if they did not know they were too ignorant to be entrusted with the affairs of the country. (Applause.) Early in 1876 Mr. Disraeli's Government circulated a balance sheet of Egypt, showing a surplus. He at once analysed it and in the last week of January, or the first week in Feb- ruary, 1876, he published that analysis, and showed that they had made a surplus by making the income two or three millions too much, and the expenditure two or three millions too little. (Laughter.) He then referred to the establish- ment of the Dual Control, and to the dethronement of Is- mael, who was then called a rascal prince. He (Mr. Brad- laugh) had said that Ismael was a rascal before that, and their Warriogton editor called him a " demagogue," and thet was the nicest ward he used. (Laughter.) But it was none of England's business to dethrone rascal princes, beceuse if It were they would fled plenty of work throughout the, world, and mach nearer hems than Egypt. (Laughter and hear, hear.) When Ismael would not pay his debts, he left Egypt one of richest men in the world. He was worth several millions at the present time, and yet he was a man who had not been able to pay Ws creditors a farthing. ('Shame.") As for Tewfik, Ismael's successor, he (Mr. Bradlaugh) knew no more about him than the Conservative editor he had referred to, and that was not much. (Laugh- ter.) They must excuse these little references as he had a ledger account open with that editor. (Loire laughter and applause.) Mr. Bradlaugh then gave a sketch of affairs in Egypt, from the institution of the Dull Control up to with- in the last few months. Referring to the commissariat ar- rangements for feeding the army of Egypt, he said that large quantities of hay were sent out which stank so badly that the horses would not eat it, and the men refused to lie on it. They sent live cattle out without making any provision for their being looked after, so that when they were landed the Arabs got them and our own men got none of them at all. (Laughter.) Carts were sent out with narrow wheels instead of broad ones, so that they stuck in the sand, and as the harness that was sent out was rotten, when the carts stuck they could not be drawn out. (Laughter.) A good deal of nonsense had been talked about the Soudan, especially by that editor to whom he referred—(laughter)--and it was lees excusable on his part because if he had ?pent 2s. SI on a little report made by the late unfortunate Lieut.-Col. Stewart —(applause)--he would have found practically everything that it is possible to tell about it at the present moment. Therefore when they saw that editor writing about a stable Government for the Soudan, they must remember that the Soudan was rather bigger than the whole of Hindostan and there were millions of its inhabitants whose habits they d d not even know. They described the Arabs as "rebels," but he could not tell against whom they were rebels. They were not rebels against Te wfik, because they bad never accepted his authority, not against the English G overn ment, because they had never had any autbcrity in the Souilan, and not even against Ismeel for he bad no authority except in three or four cities, which beheld by his troops, and outside these no auth- ority whatever. The way in which he collected taxes washy stealing and marauding. When General Gordon was there in 1874 the only way in whicl. he collected taxes was by selling the flocks and herds of the people. He (Mr. Brad- laugh) did not allege that there was any harm in that, be- cause General Gordon defended it in his own words, but that was the way taxes were collected, and Gordon was one of the best governor., so they might think what the worst were. (Hear, hear.) Unfortunately they commenced meddling in the gouclan whilst all the time repudiating meddling. General Gordon was sent out with instructions to give effect to the abandonment policy, and they had itin his own words that he accepted the mission the Government gave him. When he got there, however, he changed his mind entirely, and he (Mr. Bradlaugh) said that when a man accepted a mission from a Government he had no right to change his mind. (Hear, hear.) It was right that he should say he had the most thorough conviction of the full ,and conplete physical bravery of General Gordon, but that was not enough. When Gordon got to the Soudan he published a procla- mation stating that henceforth no one should interfere with their property, and whoever had slaves in his services should have the right to their services and full control over them without any interference whatever. Having a large sum of money with him which he took from England for the pur- pose of abandoning the Soudan ; directly he got there he laid out the money in the purchase of negro slaves, whom without their consent he made Into an army to fi4ht for him It was not the first time he had done that. He did it in 1876 and 1877 and justified it ever and over again With regard to slavery Gordon said If a father or mother, of their own free will and with the will of the child, seld that child he did not see any objection to it." They might judge what free will the child had. (Hear, hear.) Gordon also said that one man brought two of his own children and sold them to him. He gave one of these to a man whose name he did not mention, and the other to a German. With re- gard to the soldiers. Gordon asked bow they were to recruit if the slave trade ceased, and he said that though the slaves

might not like to serve in the army against their wills, the same thing happened in countries in which there was con- scription. (Hear, bear.) On one occasion be optured a slave-dealer's convey of men and women slaves. The %en and boys be put into the army and the women he told off to be wives for the men. (" Shame.") And that night be was disturbed by a noise' and, to use his own words, he found that the lots were being " scrambled" for. (" Shame.") Ha (Mr. Bradlaugh) thought when they were applauding Gordon as a hero they ought to remember some of these things. (Applause.) Gordon sold his services to the Chinese to fight against the rebels there ; be sold his services te Ismael for several years, and they had it in his own words that be would resign his office if it did not pay hint. There was certainly ne affection for the Soudanese, fer he said at one time that he wished they had but one neck that he might break it. And, finally, he was going to sell his services to the King of the Belgians to govern the Congo Free Stsres. (Applause.) Mr. Bradlaugh then went on to condemn secret diplomacy and to advocate a complete withdrawal front the Soudan. (Applause.) in conclusion he invited questions. Mr. DUNBOBBIN asked what had Weems of Mr. Newde- gate. (Laughter.) Mr. BRADLAUGH said that was not the question that night, and he should be exceedingly sorry to say anything against Mr. Newelegate at that moment, because he had reason to believe he was ill and it would be unmanly to attack him. (Applause.) As there was no more questions asked, he thanked them for listening to him, and as the Conservatives in the town had not taken that opportunity of sneaking, be hoped they would mend their language in the future. (Ap- plause.) The meeting then ended.

THE CHARGE OF EMBEZZLEMENT AT WARRINGTON. At IVarengton Borough Court on Monday, Harold Booth Quarmby, formerly clerk in the employ at the Florence Hill Company, was brought before the magistrates on remand and charged with falsifying the books of his em- ployers, the Florence Mill Company, Limited, at divers dates during the last two years.—Mr. Ridgway appeared on behalf of the company, and Mr A. Browne defended pri- soner.—Mr. Ridgway said that the books elf the company had not yet been completely audited, and at a meeting of the directors held the other evening the matter was thor- oughly gone into as regarded the stare of the books and the charge made against Quarmby. He was instructed by the directors to ask their worships to approve of the defendant being let out on bail, te come up when called upon, as the directors were of opinion, and be might say he was of opinion, that in the interests of justice it would be better for all parties implicated to be charged together, rather than come under separate charges.—Mr. Browne said he consented with every readiness to what Mr. Ridgway pro- posed. As to whether or no sureties would be rrquired was left to their worships, but they would know that it was almost impossible for a man in the present prisoner's posi- tion to get sureties, be having been in custody a fortnight with such charges hanging over him. He suggested that prisoner be allowed free on his own recognisances.—Mr. Ridgway thought it was right to tell the Bench that Quarmby had given assistance to the auditors in going through the audit up to the present, and no doubt suca assistance would again be required.—Mr. Browne: This bail, if sureties were required, will. lithe other persons are not apprehended, last for ever.—The Mayor (Alderman Harrison) : Of course, the other delinquent is beyond the seas.—Mr. Ridgway said that he had no official knowledge of that, and it might ha more than one, so he had to speak with reserve. He suggested that there should be a limit put to the recognisances.—Mr. Hunt: I feel that it is a Case for sureties.—Mr. Browne said that the matter was in the hauds of the prosecution—Mr. Hunt: I hold some- thing in my hand that makes me feel justified in saying so. and Mr. Browne knows it does. lam held responsible in a great measure.—A document was then handed to Ridg• way, who said that jibe had known of the statement therein before he should certainly have said that tkere should be at least one surety, and substaatial bail fret prisoner. Ha did not think there would be the difficulty that Mr. Browne anticipated about the sureties, as he thought there would be some friend who would come forward.—Mr. Browne: Friends generally desert one at such times as these. —The Mayor: Sometimes; but there are excep- tions. Don't you think you can get one surety.— Prisoner: Perhaps you will accept my aunt's surety.— The Mayor: If she is a respectable person we have no ob- jection.—lt was then decided that prisoner should be liberated on his own recognisances of £2O, and one surety of £2O, to come up when called upon within the next six months.—Mr. Hunt: What is to be done with the property. I hold a considerable amount of cash. Mr. Browns: My client claims that as his own.— Mr. Ridgway : I think that should be held over in the meanwhile.—Mr. Hunt: I only want to he clear; it is no interest to me.—The Mayor : I think Mr. Hunt might be the custodian of that.—Mr. Ridgway : I should object to it being given back.—Mr. Browne : There is no charge of embezzlement, therefore this can be no part of stolen money.—Mr. Ridgway : Technically it might be the charge later on.—Mr. Hunt said that be would rather be re- lieved of the responsibility of the money.—Mr. Browne: lam afraid Mr. Hunt is looking after his own costa—Mr. Hunt: The costa are certain from the conwariy.—The Mayor said that a man could not do wrong without suffering in consequence, and they could not make an order for the money to be dealt with any other way than to remain in the hands of the chief constable. If there was no charge preferred at the ex- piration of six months, they would be open to another ap- plication.—The Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. White) explained that the original charge against prisoner was ose of embezzl- ing, in company with another, the sum of £3O, and falsifi- cation of the books was afterwards added.—Mr. Hunt : He was received in custody on his own confession.—Mr. Ridg- way: If your worships wiah to know anything further, and the defendant's solicitors do not object, I shall be willing to make a statement in the private room, but I think in the interests of justice I should not make a public one. There is nothing to conceal, but it is inadvisable to make things teo public —The Magistrates' Clerk asked would the state- meet refer to the money P—Mr. Ridgway: ro why the charge is altered.—The Magistretet' Clerk : It is open to you to prefer a similar or another charge. It is a charge stated this morning as something to work upon.—The Mayor (to prisoner) : How did you come possesed of the money that has been taken away from you ?—Mr. Browne : I do not think that is--The Mayor : We are asking it for the purpose of endeavouring to give him the advantage of the suggestion that has been made, and we only want the truth. —tar. Hunt said that the police could tell how prieoner said he became possessed of the money, but perhaps it would not be advisalle.—Mr. Browne : I believe the amount is £l3 odd. £3 of it is my client's own money.—The Magis- trates' Clerk : Is there any objection to the £3 being given him ?—Mr. Ridgway : I have a very great ohjecCon.—The Bench decreed that the money should remain in the hands of the police, and Quarmby was shortly afterwards libera- ted.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

The drying winds and the occasional glimpses of sun- shine have rendered considerable help during.the past week to destroy weeds, and the hoe has been indus- triously applied amongst the crops and other vacant spaces. Even where weeds were not actually visible, the moving of the surface soil with this implement is always beneficial to the crops as well as disturbing the germinating seeds of weeds. Therefore, :advantage should be taken of suitable weather at all times to use the hoe, for, however diligent we may be, a showery week or two would be productive of a garden covered with weeds. During such weather hoeing has very little effect, as the weeds in the majority of instances will strike fresh root if they are not moved away. We should like to see weeds thriving more than they do at the present time, for we should then feel satisfied that other tenants of the vegetable garcren were progressing. What with the frosts at night, the cutting winds, and hail showers, gardeners are nearly at a standstill so far as transplanting young seedlings and so on are concerned. Seeds that have been sown and ought to have been up long ago are still invisible. SCARLET RUNNER BBANS.—These may be sown any time now. Growing, as they do, 10 or 12 feet high, the cottager should consider before he sows them, or he may obstruct the sun's rays from half the crops in the garden. For instance, a row with ends nofth and south would cast a shadow on the east and west side. Pro- bably the best arrangement for the sake of all the other crops is to place the row of Scarlet Runners on the northern boundary of the garden, with ends east and west. In this way the garden will be fully exposed, and no land is taken up beyond a pathway on either side for the purpose of picking the produce. The next best-posi- tion would be the east or west boundary. Circular patches having a diameter of two or three feet may be dotted in convenient spaces in the garden. Round, the outside of the circle the seeds should be planted four inches distant. For the purpose of supporting them stakes from six to twelve feet may be driven in the ground, and braced together at the top so as to impart strength to the whole. Some use a strong iron hoop for the top, half the diameter of the circle at the base, and secure the supports to it with strong pieces of string, and the arrangement is well suited to short stakes. Long ones must be brought together at the top, and, in order to do this readily, the stakes must be thrust in obliquely. The beans that are supplied with the short sticks should be stopped when they have reached half- way up, or they will be too crowded if left unchecked till they reach the top. This somewhat novel plan of growing Scarlet Runners will commend itself to growers with limited space, as it combines the picturesque with the profitable.

Tiiß FRONT GARDEN.—Beyond bringing up the arrear of such work as the planting of hardy subjects, very little can be done here before we have a decided change in the weather, which, at time of writing, is most pro- mising. The ground should, however, be in readiness for bedding plants. Dahlias should have holes made for them 18 inches square, and about the same depth, which should be refilled with manure and a portion of the soil that was taken out. Into the centre of these holes the plants can be put at the proper time. Newly-planted rose trees, i.e., -those planted since last October, should have a mulching of sorno kind placed on the surface of the soil so far as their roots extend to prevent excessive evaporation from the soil and so affect the roots. Sud-

div.p: lIOUSE OF LORDS.-WEDNESDAY.

The Donee met at half-past eleven o'clock. nut REGISTRATION BILLS,—The Standing Orders were dispensed with, and offer a few words of objection from Lord Denman, the reports of amendments to the English, Irish, and Scotch Registration Bills were received, and the several bills read a third time. VOTE or Carnir BILL—The Consolidated Fund No. 3 (Tote of Credit) Bill was read a third time. The sitting was suspended during pleasure to await the return of the Registration Bills from the House of Com- MODEL

The sitting being resumed at five o'clock, the Clerk repor- ted that their Lordships' amendments to the Registration Bills had been agreed to by the Commons.—The House at once adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.
The Speaker took the chair at a quarter past twelve o'clock.

The Registration of Voters (Scotland) Bill, and the Reg- istration of Voters (Ireland) Bill also passed through Com- raittee.—The Barristers' Admission (Ireland) Bill was read a third time and passed. OPERATIONS IN EGYPT.—The Earl of JERSEY moved for a return of the total sum. spent by the Imperial and Indian Government on naval and military operations in or connected with Egypt since danaary, 1852; and also a return for the same period et the officers and men who had lost their lives, and the number invalided home in con- sequence of our operations In Egypt.—The return was ordered, and the House adjourned at 7-40.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TIIESDAY,
The Speaker took the chair shortly before four o'clock. Upwards of an hour was occupied in the discussion of pri- vate bills.
Mr. ilinszaT introduced the Princess Beatrice Annlty

THE EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY ACT.—Tn answer to Mr. C. Roundel!, the ATTORNEY-GENERAL said that baying regard to the care with which the superior courts exercised their power of removing cases under the Employers' Liability Act from the county courts, and to the fact that this w. 5 never done unless special reasons were shown, he did not think it would be desirable to amend the Employers' Liability Act so as to secure the trial before the county courts of all cases where the individual claim amounts to less than £5O.

TIIR SUARIM•BERBER RAILWAY.—III reply to Sir R. Cross Sir A. BATTU said ao telegrams had been received from Lord Wolseley during the time be was at &Islam protesting against instructions sent to him from the War Office as im- practicable from a military point of view. All important telegrams and despatches received from Lord Wolseley would be included iu the papers which would be laid on the table en an early day. COMMERCIAL RELATIONS WITH SPAIN.—III reply to Sir S. Not thoote, Mr. Hominy said that on the second reading of the Customs and Inland Revenue Bill the Chancellor of the Exchequer would state what coarse he proposed to adopt in consequence of the failure of the commercial negotia- tions with Spain. Tan Sun (Ism.—Lord E. FITAMAIIRICH informed Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett that pending the negotiations which were now going on, be was unable to make any statement with respect to the proceeding of the conference on the Saes Canal. But his refustl to give confirmation on this subject must not be taken to imply avant to inferences which might be drawn frOm the manner in which the question was ex. pressed. The House adjourned at six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.--..THIIRSDAT. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at four o'clock. MISCRLLANEOI79.—The Registration Bills and more than thirty other public and private measures received the Royal assent.—The Scetch Fisheries Amendment Bill was, on the motion of the Earl of DeLnorstx. read a second time.— Lord LAMINGTON called the attention of their lordships to the Declaration of P.ris of 1858, and moved that it is the duty of this country to withdraw from the Declaration, and thus maintain our ancient maritime rights, so essential .to ' the power and prosperity of the empire.—Tarl GRAN- TILLS replied that this and the other countries parties to the Declaration were bound by it.—The motion wan withdrawn.—The Earl of KIWIERLEY informed Lord Inchiquin that Russia had not demanded to be diplomatic- ally reprepresented at Cabal on a footing of perfect equality with England.—Earl GRANVILLII stated that there had been communications with Turkey on the subject of Sua- kim. which had led to no result; but there had been no negotiations with other Powers. Their Lordships adjourned at a quarter before seven o'clock until Friday, sth June. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Tacasnar.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. Quesetows.—Lord E. FITZMAURICE, referring to the re- appearance of the Bosphore Eyyptien, stated that the French Government had informed our Grovernmeut that positive assurances bad been given that the paper would create no difficulty by the tone of its articles, and that the editor had been warned that if he publishid any matter which would give reasonable cause of offence the French Consul would afford facilities to the Egyptian Government for the sup- pression of the paper.—Mr. J. K. CROSS informed Mr. Stan- hope that the publication of papers containing an account of the meeting between the Viceroy of India and the A meer would not be in the public interest —The PRIME MINISTER undertook that before the House was asked to read the Customs and Inland Revenue Bill a second time a clear expression of the intentions of the Government should be given with regard to the provisions alf,cting the duties en wine, spirits, and beer.—The Arromertv-Gintezean stated, in reply to a question, that clerks of the peace and town clerks must issue their precepts entirely in relation to the present state of the 14w, and regardless of the provisions of the Redistribution Bill.—Replying to Sir S. Northcete as to the change of the orders given to the Criteria, the Marquis of HARTINGTON Said he did not think it de- sirable to give any details of the reasons which had induced the Government to direct the detention I of the Guards at Alexandria for a short time. The special preparations for which a vote had been granted by the House had not been suspended, and he did not think he should state how soon the Government would consider it desirable to suspend them. All he could say was that it had been thought desirable that the brigade of Guards should remain in positions in the Mediterranean. —Mr. GLADSTONE stated that the Suez Canal negotiations at Paris had been making progress, and that the House would be put in possession of the whole information before any- thing was done. The right hon. gentleman told B iron LI de Worms that the terms of reference as to the prat:used arbitration on the Penjdeh incident were not yet definitely settled.—Sir C Dues, who was questioned as to a rumour of an outbreak of cl.olera in this country, stated that there was no foundation whatever for the rumour. EAST hum Loan. BILL.—The second reading of the East India Loan (£l0000,000) Bill was moved by Mr. J. K. Cnoss, who explained that the money was rtquired for pub- lic works. He remarked that the railways of India, which were now the property of the State, were a source of very con- rderable profit, and they now proposed an additional expen- diture on the extension of these railways to the extent of £3.500,000. The Government of India bad made a large demand for the extension of railways upon the frontier. The Government proposed first to make the defensible line of the Indus Valley absolutely impregnable. They wished also to perfect our communication with Quetta and Pishin. Ira addition to the railways' there was to be means of communication between the defensive points of the Indus Valley and the Pishin Valley in the form of a mili- tary road 250 miles long. Instead of completing the SRA- Pishin line, it was proposed in consequence of natural obstacles making it difficult of conetruction, to lay down a line through the Bolan Pass. They hoped to complete the railway to Quetta by the end of the present year, and the total cost of these frontier railways would be /-5,000,000 nominal. Part of that money would have to be found from the revenues of India and part from the loan now asked for. —Mr. E. STANHOPE had given notice of an amendment, but he withdrew his opposition to the bill, and recommended the Government to finish the Quetta railway as soon as they could, contending that its abandon- ment in 16lt0 was a blunder committed in defiance of Indian military and political opinioc—Sir G. CAMPBELL asserted that the Government abandoned the railway in order to win the applause of Lancashire by the abolition of the import duties on Lancashire goods.—Mr. SLAGG said he failed to see the connection between the two things. With regard to the vast expenditure now proposed, he feared that when another Government came into office a tetally different scheme would be presented, all would be changed, and the outcome would be an immense victimisation of the people I of India and an increase of their burdens.—After a long dis- cussion, the Bill was read a second time. THE WHITSUNTIDE HOLIDAYS.-0a the motion for the adjournment of the House for the Whitsun holidays, Sir Walter Barttelot and Mr. Chaplin criticised the policy of the Government. Mr. Gladstone, in a speech delivered in a , conversational tone, in a thin House, touched various points raised. With respect to Russia, he admitted that the pro- ceedings for the settlement of the frontier had not gone forward as he had desired. There WAS in Russia, as he feared there was in this country, a party who did not work for peace—a remark much cheered by the Liberal side. He could not undertake to say when the negotiations would be closed, but he declared that the Government were pressing forward with steadfastness the policy of a long succession of English statesmen, one which he believed had the con- currence of national feeling. At a quarter to one the motion for the adjournment over the Whitsuntide holidays was agreed to, and, the remaining orders disposed of, the House adjourned.

div.head: ENGLAND AND RUSSIA.
div.p: ENGLAND AND RUSSIA.
PROCLAMATION BY THE AMEER. HONOURS FOR GENERAL KOMAROFF.

- - Ceicyrra, Sus/P.m—The question of native volunteering for the defence of English rule ia India is to come before the Viceroy in Council shortly. In the meantime, the native press strongly urges upon the Imperial Government to grant the concession. At Deogurh, which is one of the seven holiest shrines in India, a greet procession of puodite and priests is being organised. Prayers are to he offered for the preservation of peace‘between England and Russia and for a blessing on the Queen. Such a ceremony in al- most if not quite unprecedented in the history of English rule in Asia,

TIRPI74 WBDSZSDLY.—The Amer has issued a procla- mation complimenting his troops on their gallantry at Penjdeb, and laying great stress on the value of the British alliance. Reinforcements arrive at Herat daily. General Komaroff recently visited the Russian outposts, but appi- rently without ostentation. He has since left for Askabad, and Colonel Alikanhoff is now at Merv. It would be better for the prospects of peace were the latter at Copenhagen. All is well and quiet here. _ .

Sr. PETERSII7RO, SATITADAY.—The Emperor has ad- dressed an autograph letter to General Komaroff, accom- panviag the gift of a gold sword of honour, the hilt and scabbard of which are set with diamonds. His Majestv warmly acknowledges what the letter dessribes as the General's excellent military measures while commanding the detachment on the Marghab, the prudence and firmness with which he dealt with the Afghans, and the gallantry which be displayed during the engagement at Dash Kepri. The Emperor has also conferred a gold sword of honour upon Colonel Zakrejevaki, as a reward for bravery. The German St. Petersburg Gazette states that it has been decided to continue the Trans-Caspian Railway within the next two years through Bukhara as far as Samar- cand.

COLLECTION OF STORES AT QuETTA._ _

Szsaso, TUSSDAY.—It— has been decided that the three months' stores collected for the Army Corps recently formed, in view of the contingency of an Anglo-itu.eian war, shall be permanently stocked at Quetta. The, Indian Govern- ment has under consideration the question of making pro- vision for the larger employment in the army of natives of good position. TEHERAN, THITIMDAY. Advices received here from Sarakbs state that, owing to the overfitiv of the Tieden Te• jen river, the direct roads to Mery are impassable. The Governor of Sarakhs received a letter on May 9 from the Russian military commander at Mery asking permission for SORle Russian troops to march along the left bank of the Tejen river, which is Persian territory, and over the bridge situated a short distance below Slrakhs. The Governor granted permission for the passace of two battalions to re- inforse the garrison of Merv, which was availed of by the Russian commander.

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.
THE SOUDAN
GENERAL °RIM; BY LORD WOLSELEY.

&TAMIL, SIII(DAY.—Lord Wolmlay has issued the follow- ing special general order to the soldiers, sailors, and marines of the army in the Soudan :—" lier Majesty's Government having decided to withdraw most of she troops from the Soudan, I desire, when bidding you farewell, to express to all my deep sense of your admirable conduct. The army in the Soudan has not only fought with courage and firmness, and cheerfully borne no small amount of hardship, it has shown, in addition, qualities higher even than those required for the patient endurance of privation, for the defeat of the bravo but cruel enemy with wh rn it has been engaged. Crime has been almost unknown in its rank', the highest standard of discipline has been maintained, and the beha- viour of all the troops—British. Indian. and colonial—bas been in every way creditable to them and to the services to which they belong. My beet thanks are due to all ranks of the Royal Navy and Marines, who have taken part in the recent campaign in the Soudan. Where bard work or hard fighting was to be done the men of these services were to be found, and I am at a loss to say whether they were more re- markable for their hard work or for their hard fighting. From the beginnime of the operations last September to the present date officers and men of the Navy had been untiring in their exertions, and all they bad to do has been done effec- tively and well. I would also thank the gallant soldiers of the New South Wales Contingent not only for the services they have rendered, but also for the sympathy which promp- ted them to come from afar to Cake part in a war undertaken by the Empire to which we all belong. They will carry home with them the thanks of our Sovereign and the best wishes of those with whom they have fought side by side here. They have borne themselves well both in action and in camp, and I trust that should any serious war be forced upon our Empire in the future, we may again find ourselves shoulder to shoulder with Australian troops, facing a com- mon enemy. The deeds of the force in the Soudan have added one more chapter to the glorious record of our national prowess, and all of you who have belonged to it— soldiers and sailors, British, Indians, and Australians—may feel with pride the high reputation of our army and navy has gamed and not suffered at our hands. Among the many and varied memories of the recent campaign, the remem- brance of your keen eoldier-like spirit will be pleasantest to dwell upon. I shall always feel proud of having commanded you. (Signed) WOLSKLEY, General.—Suakim, 113th May. 1885.

Snextat, TINSDAY.—Lord Wolslev sailed this morning in the hired transport Queen, with the members of his personal staff, including Lord Charles Beresford, General Sir John McNeill, and Lord Wiltshire. There were also 09 men. The sth Lancers will embark on board the Lydian Monarch to- morrow. One squadron of the Bengal Lancers remains here as part of the permanent garrison, the remainder returning he India shortly. Major-General Sir G. Greaves assumed command here yesterday. General Lord Wolseley telegraphs : " Snakim, Sunday, 2-40 p.m.—Following from Intelli- gence Department, Dongela :—Vakil, from Dongola, re- ports that Sennaar Mudiryeh is cleared of the rebels. Khalifa Abdulla Taashi dead of smallpox. In the battle near Rabad, Kordofan, when Abu Anga was beaten, many of his soldiers deserted to the enemy. All 'Limas Arabs in revolt against tbe Mandi, who has very few men indeed with hint. Everything we hear points to the Mandi being in great straits." DEPARTURE OF GENERAL GRAHAM.

SUAKIN. SATUBDAY.—GeneraI Graham left here- at five o'clock to inspect the Berkshire Regiment. He compli- mented the men highly on their conduct, mentioning in par- ticular Colour-Sergeant Cloke for distinguished gallantry, which he stated would be brought to the notice of her Majesty. General Graham then rode to Ofao, and bade farewell to the Shropshire Regiment. The Scots Guards to-day returned from Tambouk and embarked on board the Jumna. In addition to the Grenadiers and Scots Guards, this vessel will take ninety invalids and General Freersantle. This evening General Graham inspected the Indian contin- gent. He warmly praised the troops for their gallant beha- viour under all circumstances.

Stumm, SawDAY.—The Jumna, with General Freemantle and Scots and Grenadier Guards; and the Deccan, with General Graham and staff, mad a number of other officers, sailed this morning. The further evacuation of Suakim is suspended for the present. Swum, MONDAY.— ('he Arab, with the Australian C)n- tingent, bag just steamed down the harbour. The Austra- lians were greeted with cheering from the transports, and heartily responded. The colonial soldiers' were clastered thickly on the deck as the vessel passed the Queen steamer, when they renewed their farewell cheers, the band playing " God save the Queen." Lord Wolseley inspected the Indian Contingent this morning. The Commander-in- Chief spoke in the highest terms of the appearance and efficiency of the force, and thanked the officers and men for their gallant and cheerful performance of the arduous dutiee committed to them.

DONGOLA. SIINW.Y.—A. spy from Khartoum reports that Alxlulla Taub', the fdandi's chief Khalita and the moving spilt of the rebellion, has died of smallpox, and that his followers have been dispersed. The Siudiryeh of Sennaar is now free from rebels, consequent upon the late engage. ment with the garrisons. DONGOLI. TUBSDAT.—The evacuation of the Soudan by British troops begins en the 21st inst. All merchants and many others are leaving. Abu Anga, the lidandi's General, has been defeated in Kordofan, and with the survivors of his force has joined the enemy at Jabal Dayer. Cam, WIDIRSDAY.—The Military police and invalids have commenced their journey down the Nile from the Snidan. It is expected that the British garrison at Cairo will be increased.

The Bosphore Etyptien re•appaared this afternoon. FOI7AICIItt THIIRSDAY.—GeseraI Greaves has determined, in conerquence of the attitude of the marauders yesterday, to resume night patrolling on the railway, by means of the armoured trains. About eleven o'clock last night the train ran to Ot4o. The enemy threw earth and brushwood on the line and also cut the telegraph wire, where the darkness of the night enabled them to do so unperceived. The train returned unmolested, the obstruction being easily removed. DEPARTURE OF REFUGEES.

DONSOLA, THURSDAY EYE/MM.—TN evacuation of the Soudan may be said to have commenced in earnest to-day, when the srat batch of refagees and natives who fear to re- main behind after the departure of the British troops started for Upper Egypt. The party numbered 520 persons. ITALY AND ENGLAND.

Rout, MONDAY—La Tribune states that DO decision has yet been taken with regard to an occupation of Suakim by Italian troops. The Journal adds that Signori Depretis and Mancini have had two interviews at Naples with Sir Savile Lumley, who to-day conferred with Signer Malvan°, Director-General in the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. Signor Depretie yesterday received Generals Blain and Ricotti, who declared that they were prepared to undertake the omipation if Suakim. A decision is expected to be ar- rived at after the Ring's return from Naples. THE SUEZ CANAL COMMISSION. PARTS, MONDAY—The sub-committee of the filßeZ Canal Commission to-day passed the aenond reading of the draft treaty. The remainder will be dealt with to-morrow. The plenary Cflumission will be summoned to meet on the 25th instant. Unless there be a material change in the attitude of England or the Foreign Power, the commission will break en without result ; and up to the present there are no signs of any concessions being made on either side. div.head: RIEL.
div.p: RIEL.

_ OTTAWA, SATIRDAY.—RieI was captured yesterday even• ing, and brou4ht to General Middleton's tent. When he, Dumont. and three others fled after the battle, three scouts, who were seperated from the main body of the troops and were coming out of the bush, espied Riel, and summoned him to surrender. The rebels, however, fired at the scouts, and cantinued their flight on hotseback. The scouts then gave chase, and succeeded in capturing Riel. In order to conceal him from the wrath of the troops, he was concealed in a coulee until General Middleton had been informed of
his capture. The troops were then ordered to their tents, and Rid l was brought into camp. Dumont has not yet been taken.

Orrawa, TIIESDAY.—The transport service between swift Current and Battleford has been suspended, as the Indians are reported to be on the trail for the purpose of plundering supplies. Col. Otter's march from Bettleford against the Indians, and the severe blow administered in subsequent fighting, have prevented many Indians from joining the rebels.

div.p: FRANCE AND SPAIN.

MADRID, MONDAY.—The Spanish African Society has received serious reports from its representatives in the Gulf ef Guinea, stating tbat a French gan boat recently entered the rivers Mini and Noya, and hoisted the French nag in several villages forming part of the territory acquired by the Spanish Society in November last. FRANCE AND CHINA

Penis, SATUBDAY.—The report of the Committee upon the Egyptian Financial Convention recommends its adop- tion by the Chamber. It is announced from Tientsin that negotiations commenced there between Li Hung Chang and M. Patene,tze on the 11th inst., and have since con- tinued regularly. FRANCE AND CHINA.

Penis, Tuttasney.—A telegram (rem Tientsin of to-day's data announces that negotiations continue on a very friendly footing between M. Patenotre and Li Hung Chang, and that an agreement has ben arrived at upon eight of the points requiring settlement. Only two points now remain under discussion.

Sir H. Maxwell, a Scotch member, has created some sur- prise in the House of Commons by giving notice that he will move the rejection of the Crofters Bill. THE ROBBERY AT THE VOTE OFFICE OF THE Howse OF COMMONS.—One of the men employed as cleaner at the House of Commons was taken into custody on Wednesday on suspicion of being concerned in the recent robbery of a cashbox' with £6O, from the Vote Office. The man, Trios. Marton by name, was brought before Mr. D'Eyncourt, at Westminster Police Court, on Wednesday afternoon, and charged by Chief Inspector Denning with the offence. Mr. Denning said suspicion attached to Morton bectuee of par- ticles of metal being found adhering to a coalpick used by the accused, and from the fact that the box was broken open with a similar instrument. Morton, who denied all knowledge of the robbery, was remanded.
