EMIL!, MONDAY.—The Duke of Connaught will leave India for England on a two months' leave on the 26th. ENGLAND AND SPAIN.

MADRID, WEDNESDAY.—Tbe Liberal papers to-day ex- press regret at the rupture of the treaty negotiations with England. They describe it as entirely unexpected, and point out the serious damage to Spanish interests resulting from the non-fulfilment of the modus roivendi, as many firms, regarding it as certain to be carried out, bad made their arrangements sccordinly. CAPTAIN BOYTON'S FREAK.

NEW YORE. TUESDAY NIGHT.—The freak perpetrated the other night by Boyton in attaching a dummy torpedo to the spar protecting the bow of Her Majesty's ship Garnet, in New York Harbour, has led to an official inquiry. The result is that Lientsnast Gardner, who prematurely released Boyton after he had been apprehended, is to be tried by court-martial. The man who was on duty as sentry at the time, and who failed to detect Boyton's approach, has been tried and sentenced to 42 days' close oonfluement.—Standard.

TIIE REVISED OLD TESTAMENT. The complete fruit of the labours of the two companies cf revisers of the Old and New Testament Scriptures, ap- pointed 15 years since, was issued to the press on Friday evening, alhough it was not on sale to the booksellers until Tuesday. The Revised Version of the Neve Testament was given to the world on May 17th, 1881, and thus, as nearly as possible, four years have elapsed between the publication of that volume and of the Revised Version of the Old Testa- ment which is now under notice. Great precautions had been taken to prevent any copies of the sacred volume get- ting into circulation, the Archbishop of Canterbury being the only personage outside the company of revisers who was permitted to have one, and it was not until Friday that the Queen was presented with the new version. It was a hand- somely bound copy of the "Standard Edition " (pica, royal Bvo., five volumes), encicsed in a morocco box, and bearing the following inscription : "Presented to her Moat Gracious Majesty the Queen by the Convocetien of the Province of Ceaterbury.-51ay xv., MDCCCLISIV." • The preface, which is dated " Jerusalem Chamber, Westminster Abbey, 20th July, 1834," sets forth the bases upon which the revisers have proceeded in their task. The main paints of this are that they have endeavoured to in. troduca as few alterations as possible into the text of the Authorised Version consistently with faithfulness," and to limit as far as possible the expression of such alterations to the language of the Authorised and earlier English versions. They state that in trying to carry out as fully as possible the spirit if these rules, which were laid down for their I guidance by the Revision Committee of Convocation, they ; have borne in mind that it was their duty not to make a new translation, but to revise one already existing, which for more than two centuries and a half had held the posi- tion of an English classic. They have, therefore, departed from it only in cases where they disagree with the transla- tors of 1611 as to the meaning or construction of a word or sentence, or where it was necessary for the sake of uniform- ity to reader such parallel passages as were identical in the Hebrew by the same English words, so that an English reader might know at once by comparison that a difference in . the translation corresponded to a difference in the original, or where the !antra:Lege of the Authorised Version was liable to be misunderstood by reason of it being archaic, or obscure, or finally, where the rendering of an earlier I English version seemed preferable, or where, by an ap- parently slight change, it was possible to bring out more fully the meaning of a passage of which the translation was already substantially accurate. The revisers go on to explain in detail their reasans for following the wage of the Authorised Version in regard to the word "Jehovah," for everywhere changing "the taber- nacle of the congregation "to "the tent of meeting," for al- tering " meat offering " to "mccl offering.," for using the I Hebrew word "eheol " in many cases where " hell "is used In the Authorised Version, and the Hebrew word " astereh " for" grove." It is added that "in regard to the language I of the Authorised Version the revisers have thought it no part of their duty to reduce it to conformity with modern usage, and have therefore left untouched all archaisms, I whether of language or of construction, which, though not in familiar use, cause a reader no embarrassment, and lead I to no misunderstanding." The old division of the books Into chapters and verses, it is further notified, has been abandoned in favour of the arrangement in paragraphs, the numbering of the chapters and verses being, however, re- tained for convenience of reference ; while in the poetical portions, besides the division into paragraphs, the revisers have adopted an arrangemett in lines, so as to exhibit the parallelism which is characteristic of Hebrew poetry. The question which will first occur te many readers is as to the manner in which the proverbial expressions—those most familiar to all of English speech—are dealt with. Without attempting to note the majority of these, it cannot escspe the attention of even a cursory reader that the ex- pressiop of Job's w eh, "Oh that mine adversary had written a book" (chapter xxxi., 35), has been changed to— "Oh that I bad the indictment which my' adversary had I written ;" that the equally familiar exclamation of David,l "I said in my haste, all men are liars" (Psalm exvi. v. 111, has become—" I saidiehen I made haste to escape all my I enercies ;" while such a time-honoured quotation as that from Genesis (chapter vii., 4), "There were giants in the earth in those dap," is now "the nephelim were in the earth In those days." Other expressions of similarly frequent use for visitation have had to be corrected by the revisers. Reuben is no longer to'd (Genesis, chapter xlix , verse 4) " Unetab!e as water, then shalt net excel," bat " Unstable as water, have nut thou the excellency." It is no more to be said, " Happy is the MU that heti' his quiver full of I them " (Pselm cxxvii., v. 5), but" Happy is the man that I bath filled his quiver with them ;" and instead of "Vanity i and vexation of spirit," we have now to read," Vanity and a striving after wind." But it is not to be conjered that all such proverbial expressions have been altered, for, In flee a majority of the most familiar have been left untouched, the revisers not having, by altering some trifling word, broken the rhythm without bettering the sense. The earliest verse of both Authorised and Revised Ver- sions is the aims: "In the beginning God created the Heaven and the earth." The first alteration occurs in the seoond verse where, instead of "And the earth was without I form, and void." we now read "And the earth was waste and void." A more striking alteration in the account of the aeration is that the formula, "And the evening and the morning were the first day," becomes "And there was evening and there was moraing one day," and " There was evening and there was morning a 'mend day," and se through the weA. The remainder of the story of the crea- tion is little changed, and the same may be said of the description of the Fall and the Flood, and the other main incidents of Genesis ; or, in fact, of the whole Old Testament. In the case of the Ten Commandments there are only a

few alterations, and these are but verbal, the most striking being that of the sixth commandment, "Thou shalt not kill" (Exodus xx. 13) becomes "non shalt do no mur- der," this being an obvious return to an older version, the commandment being given in this fashion in the book of Common Prayer. It may be noted, however, that the fifth coalmandment—" Honour thy father an thy mother that thy days may be long in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee,"- as it etinds in the Prayer Book, is, " Houenr
thy father and thy mother that thy days may be long upon the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee" in both the Authorised and the Revised versions.
The alteration which will create most attention le, in fact,

the one already noted, namely, that of giving all the poetl: cal portions in poetic form. The song of Miriam, the bless- ing of the Israelits by Balaam, the adjuration of Joshua to the Sun and Moon to etsnd still, and all similar passages are set out line by line; as also is the Book of Job, which is
treated as one long poem. the first two chapters and a por- tion of the last being all that is given as prose. The Psalms and the Proverbs are similarly dealt with, as . _ _ .

Is the Song or Solomon, as it is called ia the Authorised Version, a title which has now to give place to " The Song of Songs," the first verse justifying, 'as it does, each title, "The Smg of Songs, which is Solomon's," being the same in each version. "The Psalms " (not The Book of Psalms " as of old) are divided into five books, Book I. comprising those from the first to the forty-first, Book 11. those from the forty-second to the seventy-second, Book 111. those from the seventy-third to the eighty-ninth, Book IV. those from the ninetieth to the 106 h, and Book V. the re- mainder. The previous headings of the individual Psalms, where such have appeared, are retained, and the only change hkely to strike attention is that the instruction " Seelah," which often occurs, is now placed in smaller type and in parentheses, instead of being run on as an integral portion of the text. As in the Authorised Version, the books of Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, Jeremi.th, and the remainder of the Prophets are set . _

Vile succeeding one in Genesis and the preceding one in Malachi) shows sine of alteration. The alteration in the case of tienesis has already been given, aid for the sake of comparison the two concluding verses in the Old Testa- ment may ba extracted from each version. In the author- ised they run thus ; " Behold, I will send you Elijah the Prophet lefore the coming of the great and dreadful day of the Lord; and he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers, lest I come and smite the earth with a curse." In the Re- vised Version they are rendered thus : "behold, I will send you Elijah the Prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord come; and be shall turn the heart of the fathers to tbe children, and the heart of the children to their fathers, lest I come and smite the earth with a curse."

The attention of a vast number of readers will be given to the textual alterations, in many ctses minute, bat still easily noted by those accustomed to the rea4ing of the Scriptures. Upon examination, it will be seen that the Revisers have been remarkably free from a love for mere alteration. Two instances of this may be adduced. The fifty-third ckapter of Isaiah, commencing, "Who bath be- lieved our report? and to whom hath the arm of the Lord been revealed ? " is probably as well known as any chapter In the whole of the prophecies. In the first six verses the only alteration not merely verbal to be noted is—',And as one frorn whom men hide their face," instead or "And we hid as it were our faces from him." In the seventh verse the altera- tion is more striking :—" He was oppressed, yet he humbled himself and opened not his month as a lamb that is led to the slaughter and as a sheep that before her shearers is dumb—yea, he opened not his mouth," taking the place of "lie was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so be openeth not his mouth." The eighth verse is similarly to be noted, appearing in the Revised Version as "By oppression and judgment he was taken away, as from his generation, who among them considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living : for the transgression of my people Was he stricken:" while in the Authorised ersion it ran thus He was taken from prison and from judgment : and who shall eeclare hie generarion ? for he was cut off out of the Land of the living : for the transgression of my people was be stricken." The remainder of the alterations in this chap- ter, however, are very slight, and the same Int), be said of the favourite fifty-fifth chapter of the same prophet, com- mencing in both versions, "Ho, everyone that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that huh no money, come ye, buy and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price. ' . . . . _ _

It is the same with the twenty-third Nairn, tt. The Lord is my shepherd ; I shall not want." In the six verses there are but two alterations. Ia the third verse the statement, "He leadeth me in righteousness for His name's tisk'," be- comes "He guideth me ; " while in the fifth verse the pre- sent tense, " Thou annointest my head with oil," is changed to the past," Thou host annointed."

, Some cariosity will naturally be felt as to the manner in which the Revisers have dealt with obsolete words; and on this point, slightly touched upon above, their words in the preface may ba quoted. The principle by which they have been guided has been clear and consistent. Whore an archaic word or expression was liable to be misunderstood, or, at least, was not perfectly intelligible, they hiVe substi- tuted for it another in equally good use at the time the Authorised Version was made, and expressing all that the archaism was intended to convey, but more familiar to the modern reader. In such cases the gain was greater than the loss, but in other instances, where the word or expression, although obsolete, was not unintelligible, it was thoughtthe change would involve greater loss than gain, and the old rendering was, therefore, allowed to stand. More especially was this the case when the archaism was a perfectly c rrect rendering of the original, and there was no exact modern equivalent for it. The principle adopted by the Company will be best illustrated by instancing t To typical examples. I The veils "to ear" in the sense of "to plough," and the sub- stantive " earing " for "ploughing," were very reluctintly ' abandoned, and only because it was ascertained that their meaning was unknown to many persons of good intelligence and education. But it was easy to put in their place equoca- lents which had a pedigree of almost equal antiquity, and it would have been an excess of conservatism to refuse to sub- stitute for an unintelligible archaism an expression to which no ambiguity could be attached. On the other hand, the word "boiled" (Exodua ix" 31), which signifies "padded for seed," and is known in provincial dialects, has no synonym in literary English. To have discarded it in favour of a less accurate or more paraphrastic expression would have been to impoverish the language, and it was therefore left because it exactly expresses one view which is taken of the meaning of the original. The theory of the revisers in this particular rosy be tested by some instances of their practice. The word " bri- gandine "occurs only twice in the Old Testament, and both times in Jeremiah, the Hebrews being exhorted (chapter 40, verse 4) to furbish the spears and put on the " b-igan- dines;' and in the third verse of the Slat chapter the Almighty promises to raise an army against Babylon and against him that bendeth let the archer bend his bow, and "against him that lifteth himself up in his brigandine," the Revised Version has substituted "coat of mail "in each case. I For the word "Cockatrice" there has been given "Basilisk," with " adder " as a marginal alternative. "The wimples , and the crisping pins," only mentioned once (Isaiah, chapter 3, verse 22), have altogether disappeared, leaving nothing in their place. ,•Emerods" have occasionally to make way for "tumours" (Ist Samuel, chapter 5, verse 0).

STRANGE LIFE IN4...IDENTB OF THE CONVICTS. Information, from a source said to be authentic, shows that when Cunningham was about two years old his father was evic'ed from a small holding near Cork, and, together with hie wife and children, including an infant three months old, had to sleep under a hedge for three night, and in con- sequence the baby died. In after-life Cunningham emigrated to America, where he joined a Fenian organisation. He woe initiated Into its myetiries, but bad not risen to the position of centre when he was selected to take part in the winter campaign of this year, it being his first mission to this country. He had no hand In the Gower-street explo- sion ; the man who committed that entrage was his elder brother. Immediately after the outrage, Canningham was told off, as one of two men, by Barton, to commit the out- rage at the Tower. His part wee to walk in rear of his =- COM eller., and see that no one approached or interfered with the depesiting of the explcsive. Ibe " machiue" was ex- ploded by a vesuvian by which the fuse was igelted• The Nee was timed to burn fifteen minutes, so as to allow both the conspirators to get out of the Tower. But, as events have proved, Cunnigham did not escape, although his ac- compliant did, and he is now in America. The connection of Barton with the conspiracy is much more conspicuous than that of Cunningham, and he occu- pied a intich higher position in the ranks of the society. No explcsion in London, with the exception of tiat at London Bridge, has taken place without his knowledge, and gene- rally under his direction. In 1872 he went from Liverpool to America, and in 1875 he joined one of the Irish Secret Societies. He soon became a prominent member. For a cmsiderable time be was the bosom friend of O'Donovan Rona and other prominent Nationalists, and !leder. the as- sumed name of "James Feeney" was one of the most active propagators of sedition amongst the Irish residents in America. While in Baltimore it is said that he was a regu- lar visitor at the house of a hands me Quadroon lady, and that she was not oblivious to his attentions. The local I .4 patriots" could not endure tile fraternising of the Celt with the negress, and complaints were sent to New York, which resulted in the sudden recall of Burton to head- quarters, and within a fortnight after his depar- ture from Baltimore, May Smith, the young Quadroon girl, was found shot dead in one of the outekirts of that city. The exact mode of her death remains a rnyetery,but uely rumours regarding it were circulated at the time. In 1880 Burton quarrelled with Rossa, and since that date the two men have been bitter enemies. Burton joined the society of "The Sons of Freedom," and was soon promoted to one of the most important posts in that organisation. At the thee of his arrest there were only two persons his superiors in the organisation. Burton formed an association of his own —of which he was the supreme head—the "Avengers.' The members consist of the most desperate of the Irish fee- Hone, and are bound under the most fearful oaths to kill any person whom they receive orders to remote. The man O'Donnell, who shot the informer Carey, was a member of this society. The brotherhood is also sworn to avenge any brother who may be punished, and it will be surprising if the conviction of Burton is not followed by some attempt upon the life of some person or person, who have been officially connected with the prosecutions. Burton has in America the repatation of being the most cold-blooded, heartless, scheming scoundrel that this conspiracy has pro- duced. His was the master mind which directed all the proceedings in this country with regard to the arrangements for and the preparation of the explosions. He surveyed the buildings and selected the spot where the explosive ehould be laid. He superintended the preparation of the combus- tible ; he told off the men for the werk ; and having done- all this he calmly and, as be doubtless thought, securely, reniained quiescent while his miserable dupes viewed the infernal machines. It is currently rumoured in I fah circles in America that Barton has been actuated in carryine, out his schemes, not so much by an intense hatred of England, eni it time hseiste f thoe peropPerre:r n the State owneras bby gorfe e2la forrg egaoml do, amount td that a t realat Massachusetts, the title deeds of which are n his brother's name, bat which have been acquired with money that has come from the pockets of the subscribers to the associations.

div.head: SIR C. WARREN'S EXPEDITION.
div.p: SIR C. WARREN'S EXPEDITION.

CAPE TOWN, TVESDAY.--Sir Charles Warren has arrived at Abhoshong, in Khama's country. The chief Rhama hae gladly acceptkd a British protectoiate, and has placed a large tract of country, of great value, at the disposal of English settlers. The territory known as Khamee country extends as far as the Zambesi. THE FRANCHISE IN CANADA. OrrawatTllESTiAY.—The Dominion Government recently introduced a bill in the House of Commons establishing an identical franchise in all the provinces of the Dominion. The Opposition have violently opposed the measure on the grounds that each province should be free to make its own franchise, and for a month past have pursued obstructive tactics in order to prevent the bill becoming law. Some of the sittings of the House kava lasted 57 hours. The Go- vernment, however, remain firrn, and signs of collapse on the part of the Opposition are to-day apparent. ILLNESS OF PRINCE NAPOLEON.
PAWS, THORSDAY.—It is reported to-day that Prince Napoleon's state of health is such as to cause anxiety among his friend% TERRIBLE SHIPWRECKS: REAT LOSS OF LIFE.

New York papers report t—hes—u-pposed loss of two steamers, three barques. and a echooner, which are all long overdue on voyagee from various American ports to Europe. The missing veseels carried crews numbering in the aggregate more than a hundred men.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF THE ITALIAN PREMIER.
div.p: RESIGNATION OF THE ITALIAN PREMIER.

ROME, THIIRSDAL—Signor Deptkis has conveyed to the King his desire of withdrawing into private life His ex- cuses for this step are his age And his illness. Toe King, replying to the intimation, expressed his hope that if he would not remain in public life, he might live long to enjoy his repose. Signer Mancini is speken of as his successor in the Premiership.

TriE EXAMINER. , SATURDAY, MAY 23, 1885. -- 114,,,,—E Warrington Board of Guardians must felt anything but comfortable during speaking that they had last week 13— alr. HENLEY, one of HER MAJESTY'S : °Cal CI call ,-,overnment Board Inspectors. We of& Well imagine that, after hearing his tli,cial report as to the pitiable condition of Industrial Schools at Padgate, felt, as one of them •expressed it, like to tPPed dogs. These schools were intended e tr c:craimplish great things; the object in ttj.,,411g them was to keep the children 4nri'lng them from the taint of pauperism, bring them up Physically, morally, and I:1'411y in an altogether better way. There sp3,sheen no lack of funds; money has been 'riey gt freely, if not lavishly, upon them. tt 'have cost the ratepayers no less than 1114;°°Q, which at 4. per cent. means a per- -Bala-pe;nt cost of £6OO per year, apart from Got,'"es, and yet we have a report from a the",e,rnment official of such a kind as makes IritClikardians ashamed of their connection ;larthtue institution. It would seem that the lax ; "fella ent throughout has been weak and Dent regularities of various kinds have been 19. Nl`tV ; while the Medical Officer, Mr. ?een ,:31'n'rrks, has, to say the least of it, 4 nliss in attending to his duties. It advis-PLlotabie to learn that he found it N:lrin4ule to report "That, as usual in the gtilong geason, itch has made its appearance Amy gat the girls." The Inspector very pro- -1 ,4.,a5-to'n„asi. it seems to 1 us. called this an `qtl th-`• lug entry" ; and did not hesitate to pro Per at tl.e ... " disease was one which by ; ()riee.,, tendon "could be eradicated at I Llis complaint was that the children

were suffering from the itch at the beginning of the year, and that they were still suffering from the disease when he visited the school. Dr. SINKS, on being called on for an explanation, said the druggist did not know how to make the requisite lotion, and the mixture which he got from London was in- effective. He afterwards instructed the drug- gist how to make the right lotion, with the result that "one or two applications of that lotion destroyed all the insects." It is a pity that Dr. SPINS did not give the drug- gist a lesson in lotion-making a little sooner. It would have been all the better for the health of the children—to say nothing of the reputation of Padgate Schools, As the In- spector so pertinently asked, "If they could have been cured in a week, why could they not have been cured between now and Jan- uary last, and thus have prevented the spread of the disease ?" Dr, SPINKS has not as yet been able to give a satisfactory answer to this question; but we observe that, in a letter which he has made public since the meeting of the Board, he quotes Sir ERASMUS WIL- SON as an authority for the statement that among the circumstances predisposing to the development of the itch are " the spring or summer seasons." But what if the same I might be said as to the development of "the lively flea" and his " co-mates ?" Would that make them more tolerable? Would it justify their spread in any well-regulated family or institution ? We leave the Medical Officer of the Padgate Schools to furnish answers to these questions, if he likes: and, meantime, we would point out that he hasn't even the poor satisfaction of saying the itch broke out either in "spring or summer." According to his own admission, the first case occurred on the loth January—that is, in mid winter. Then, again, what are we to make of the assertion of Mr. DARBYSHIRE, (late Chairman of the Schools Committee), that "they had seldom been entirely free from the disease ?" If he was correct in making this statement—and it was made, unchallenged, in the presence of Dr. SPINKS—it would seem that there has been more than one instance of the right lotion being in the wrong place when it was wan- ted, The fact is we are driven to the con- clusion that, under the circumstances, the Medical Officer should have visited the schools oftener than once a week ; if the children had had more of the doctor they would probably have had less of the itch. The Inspector pointed out that, although a hospital was provided for isolation in case of infectious disease, it as not brought into use, and it transpired that one reason why it ; was not turned to account as intended was ; because there was no proper footpath to it. 1 On the other hand, Mr. DARBYSHIRE had to confess that the footpath had not been made because the doctor did not think the hospital had been properly built. What a confession of bungling and of failure—a ship lying idle in dock for want of a " ha'poth o' tar!" There was a disposition on the part of some of the Guardians to resent any reflection upon Mr and Mrs. MirrEs, the Superin- tendent and Matron; but Mr. HENLEY, although studiously careful as to his language, made it clear that the management was weak, adding that "he could not altogether acquit the schoolmaster of blame for the state of the es- tablishment." Indeed he went so far as to say that if the Superintendent and Matron could not look after the health of the chil- dren, and see that the place was kept clean, the sooner they made way for others and the better. The Inspector is distinctly of opinion that sufficient money is being spent on the establishment, and we dare say the ratepayers are so much of the same opinion that they will be glad if the Guardians will take the hint that has been given them to "consider if they had not more persons employed than was absolutely necessary." As things go, it would have been much better if Padgate Schools had not been built; the return for the outlay is so miserably poor. There is, however, great room for improvement ; and it is some- thing to know, on the anthority of Mr. HEN- LEY, that if the best is made of the opportu- nity, the schools may yet come to be of real service to the Warrington Union.

THosa who have day by day followed the trial of the Irish-Americans, BURTON and CUNNINGHAM, will not besurprised atits ending in their being found guilty of treason-felony, and at their being sentenced to penal servi- tude for life. The London police have been a good deal blamed for their inability to trace crimes of this description ; but credit must be given them in this instance for the skill and perseverance they have displayed, having once got a clue, in completing the chain of evidence against the prisoners. The crime with which the two men were charged was of so serious a nature that it is well it has been brought home to them with- out a shadow of doubt. They have had a fair trial—everything has been done that could be done to enable them to rebut the evidence brought against them; but they have been caught in their own net; and, being guilty of a most diabolical offence, they deserve the heavy sentence which has fallen upon them. It was shown that both prisoners had made false statements as to their visits to,England. BURTON said he had received a telegram about his brother's death, and CUNNINGHAM declared that he had come to England to see his mother, who was alleged to be living in Whitechapel ; but not a particle of evidence was adduced at the trial in support of either of these statements It was proved that the prisoners had been in communication with each other; and CUN- NINGHAM, who was at the Tower of London when the explosion took place, was the only one out of over 200 persons detained who was unable to give a satisfactory account of himself. BURTON'S connection with the at- tempted explosion at Charing Cross was of the clearest kind. Not only was the port- manteau found there which he was known to have purchased at Southampton, but in it was a coat he was observed to be wearing when he left the steamer in which he crossed from America to England. The Judge, in passing sentence, said the evidence was such as would have convicted them of high treason; and the Crown was therefore merciful in pre- senting their crime in a mitigated form. It is to be hoped, however, that the sentence will be the means of deterring others from en- gaging in the horrible work of exploding public buildings regardless of human life. Society has a tight to protect itself from wretches who are at war against it; and those who would thus destroy must take the chance of being themselves destroyed, or, as in this case, deprived of liberty to the end of their days.

WE are glad to observe that Mr. BRIGHT has, in his usual fashion, been outspoken on the question of the dowry to Princess BEATKICE. Replying to a resolution from Birmingham, asking him to oppose the vote, he says he could not condemn the present

grant on any grounds, and he adds: "If I had been in the House of Commons on Thursday last I should have voted for the grant. I would not have asked the House to cast a shadow over the mind of the QUEEN, and to tell her that in the latter years of her reign Parliament was less generous to her family than in earlier years." We can quite understand the feeling there is in some quarters that Parliament has been too ready in the past to vote grants to members of the Royal family. It may be that there has been extravagance in this direction ; but surely that is no reason why the nation should be- have shabbily in this particular instance. Because Dick, Tom, and Harry have each had,a too-large slice of sweet cake, is it fair to sister Sally that she should have none at all? Let us by all means have retrench- ment in expenditure ; but there are a hundred better ways of accomplishing it than that of making fish of one member of the Royal Family and flesh of another. If Parliament had refused the grant, it would have brought discredit upon the Crown, and through the Crown upon the nation. Mr. LABOUCIIERE may be right in his assumption that sufficient is allowed the QUEEN to enable her to provide for her family ; but if action is to be taken on that view of the matter, it should apply all round, and not operate solely against the youngest member of the family. For our own part, we feel rather grateful to the Princess that sh has stayed so long by the side of her mother. Something has been saved in that she has not been married earlier. We therefore willingly contribute the farthing we may be called upon to pay towards her dowry, and at the same time wish her all happiness.

ROUNDERS AT RUNCORN.—A rounders match was played on Saturday at Runcorn between the team of the Y.M.C.A. and a picked eleven of the Runcorn Football Club. Two innings were played with the result :—Football Club, 135 ; Y.M.C.A., 48. ST. PAUL'S CIIURCE, WIDNES.—The dedication service in connection with the new pulpit were continued on Sun- day, when the Rev. G. T. Dunne, M.A., of Barrow, preached two sermons to good congregations. Collections were made in aid of the building fund. HALEBANK WESLEYAN SUNRAY SCROOL.—The anniver- sary services connected with the Halebank Wesleyan Sun- day school were held on Sunday, when sermons were preached by the Rev. M. A. Kidman. The scholars sang special hymns, having been trained for the occasion by Mr. J. Duxbury. Mr. J. Davies preeidet at the harmonium. The total amount collected was £l2 17s 3d, RUNCORN RECREATION Foorneu, Cum.—The annual dinner took place at Mr. Arthar Riley's, Bridge-street, on Tuesday evening. There was a good number of members present, and tha proceedings were very enjoyable. It was decided to form a Rounders Club, with the following offi- cers :—T. Forster, captain ; E. Lunt, sub-captain ; T. Whinyates, hon. secretary and R. Collinge, treasurer. A RAPID RIDE TO CBESTER.—In the presence of several persons on Friday week, a Runcorn tradesman declared that he had a cob which could run to Chester attached to a two- wheeled vehicle in an hour and a half. A local publican laid a wager that the attempt would fail, and the owner and a referee shortly afterwards started. The journey, a distance of 14 miles, was accomplished in the remarkably short time of 77 minutes. RECHABITE DEMONSTRATION AT KINGSLEY.—On Monday the annual demonstration of the above society, which in this village numbers some 250 members, took place. The procession was headed by the Duddon and Kingsley Brass Bands, and, after marching through the village, the mem- bers repaired to the tent, where an excellent repast was pro- vided for them. The remainder of the day was spent in an enjoyable manner. ACCIDENT TO WIDNES CRICEETERS.-011 Satrudte, night the members of a team of cricketers belonging to the Widnes Cricket Club, who went to St. Helene to play a match with the St. Helens Recreation CIO, met with an alarming acci- dent. As they were coming down the incline from Peasley Cross their wagonette, to which four horses were attached, came in violent collision with a tramcar, and the passen- gers in both vehicles were seriouely shaken. Mr. Hayes, of Albert-road, was thrown from his seat, and had one of his arms broken. Another waggonette was procured from the Fleece Hotel, in which the party were, about midnight, driven home. SERMONS 'AND- MEETING AT FRODSIUM.—The annual sermons in aid of the funds of the Church Missionary Society were preached in the Frodshain Parish Church on Sunday be, the Rev. S. Coles, missionary from Ceylon. There were large congregations. On Monday evening the annual meeting was held in the Town Hall, Frodsham, when the Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A. (vicar), presided. The Rev, T. Neale referred to the remarkable growth of mission- ary wet k, and compared the present condition of the Church Missionary Society with what it was in 1802. The Rev. S. Coles said it was estimated there were 135 millions of Protestants, 175 millions of Mahomedans,. and 500 millions of Buddhists. A JUBILEE SERMON AT Rtneconer —An interesting ser- mon was preached in St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel oo Sun- day morning. Exactly 50 years bad elaPsed since Mr. Abraham Leach, of St. Helens, had as a fully accredited local preacher delivered his first eermon in Runcorn, and that gentleman on Sunday preached his jubillee sermon from the sixth and seventh verses of the fourth chapter of Philliplans. In the evening be preached a sermon to young men in Camden Wesleyan Chapel. Although 80 years of age, Mr. Leach's discourses were delivered in a vigorous style, and he received the hearty congratulation of a large number of friends. It is stated Mr. Leach preached the first sermon in connection with the Widtaes Wesleyan

Society. ALARMING STREET ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—About eight o'clock on Saturday evening a spring cart belonging to Mr. F. Lawrinson, grocer, Waterloo-road, was being driven along Moor-lane when the horse, a high-spirited animal, got the bit between its teeth, and slashed along at a furlong rate. The two boys in charge in their endeavours to stop the horse in its career, pulled the bridle over its head. The horse swerved and one of the wheels coming in contact with the kerbstone the animal was thrown violently to the ground, and the cart overturned. One of the boys had pre- viously jumped from the vehicle and he escaped with a few scratches, but the other was thrown violently to the ground and was somewhat seriously injured. The horse was very badly hurt about the head, and in about 20 minutes died through loss of blood from wounds on the nostrils. FAILURE OF A WIDNES TRADESMAN.—At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, on Thursday, Charles Johnson Sutcliffe, described as a plumber and painter, of 30, Victoria-read, Widnes, and who stated that he had also carried on busi- ness as a herb doctor at Blackburn, came up for public examination. The statement of affairs showed liabilities £332 12s ffil, and assets k 236 Ha 9d, a deficiency of £95 14s. The debtor ascribed his failure to bad trade, and to his losses on the business which he carried on at 18, Union-street, Blackburn, as a herbalist. He had been in this business for fourteen months and had lost £6O. He had no knowledge of the complaints of human beings, and only carried on the business as it was carried on before he took it. He did not know whether the public knew that he had no knowledge of complaints—he only followed the re- cipes he had acquired with the business. The examina- tion was adjourned to the 11th of June. NORTHWICH DIVISION LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—A meeting of the Executive Committee of this association was held in Bethesda School-room, Runcorn, on Saturday afternoon. Mr. T. Norman presided. It woe unanimously decided to invite Mr. Robert Verdin, of The Brocklehurst, Northwicla, to become president of the association, and a deputation was appointed to wait upon him. Mr. Robert Shaw, of the Highlands, Runcorn, was enthusiastically elected to the position of chairman of the Executive Committee on the proposition of the Rev. W. Gelley, of Northwich. Mr. Shaw reluctantly accepted the position. Mr. W. Handley, of Runcorn, was appointed registration agent and secretary. It was decided to hold meetings in different parts of the division for the purpose of appointing local registration agents and to transact other business. The following gen- tlemen were appointed vice-presidents i—The Rev. F. Carter, Northwich ; Mr. T. H. Forger, and Mr. Robert Hickson, of Winningten ; and Mr. G. Z. Davies, Runcorn. DEATH OF INSPECTOR Durron. FORMERLY OF RUNCORN AND LYMM.—The death took place on Wednesday, at the Polic3 Station, Egremont, of Inspector Henry Dutten for many years one of the best known officers in the Cheshire constabulary. Mr. Dutton, who was 59 years of age, had been in delicate health for the greater part of a year past, owing to an affection of the stomach, and though he discharged hie official duties to the last in the hope that he might regain his former robustness, he gradually got weaker. He was highly respected by the magistrates and others who had occasion to do business in the Liscard Police Court, where be has for a number of years been stationed as ths inspector in charge. Indeed, he was a model police-officer, and an ex- cellent pattern for the younger members of the force to imitate. Mr. Dutton was for cmsiderably over 30 yeare connected with the police force in different parts of the country, having been for five years in early life in the Liverpool force. Afterwards be joined the old Cheshire constabulary, and on the re-construction of that force in 1837 he was appointed sergeant, and was stationed at Lymm. Subsequently be was appointed inspector at North- wich, and afterwards at Runcorn, and a few years ago he was made detective-inspector for the Wirral division. Lat- terly he held the imporZant position of divisional inspector at Egreflont, where his excellent knowledge of police law was much appreciated.

CHURCH RESTORATION.—About one hundred years ago a celebrity was born in Runcoru, who afterwards assisted very much in passing the Reform Bill of 1832. William Lewis Trelawny, at one time "Captain Selusbury." His father was the late Revd. Sir Harry Trelawny, Bart. Sir William was afterwards Lord-Lieutenant of Cornwall, al- ways a great supporter of the Liberal party and useful in his generation. He was a member of Parliament and chair- man of Grand jury, and of the Board of Guardians. His youngest daughter, Mrs. Batchelor, is working hard in a very poor put of Cornwall, near the Camelford Moore, seeking to promote education; to raise the tone among her poor neighbours, and to repair and in part rebuild a hand- some old Parish Moors in the Cornish wilds. SiR RICHARD CROSS AND THE MARE'S NEST.-1 London correspondent says :—Sir Richard Cress has discovered another mare's nest. This comes in succession to the fable about Lord Dufferin so seriously differing with the policy ' of the Government in respect of the Afghan frontier that he had resigned. Sir Richard Cross had been informed in the tittle tattle that goes forward over well-appointed dinner' tables in London, and is circulated at clubs and messes, that Lord Wolseley had sent to the War Office a strong I protest against the instructions forwarded for his eeceral guidanca of military operations, and as to the disposal and withdrawal of troops in the Soudan. These instructions were, Lord Wolseley is alleged to have said, not only foolish and impolitic, but impracticable from a military point of view. Sir Richard Cross, an ex-Cabinet Minister, did not hesitate to assume the correctness of this gossip, and upon it framed a question publicly addressed to Lord Hartington. In his absence, Sir Arthur Hayter returned the simple answer that no such message had been received, at which dead silence reigned in the Conservative camp. THEFT OF A PORSF.—Rachael Connolly, a woman with a young child upon her arm, was brought up at Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday charged with stealing a parse and £1 4s. 7il , the property of Mrs. Ada Mellon, wife of the proprietor of the Theatre Royal, Widnes.—lt appeared that on Saturday afternoon Mrs. Mellon entered a public-house in Wellington-street, kept by Mr. Gill, and had a glass of stout. She was sitting down near the prisoner, who was the only other person in the room. After the prisoner had left she missed her purse and money. The prisoner subse- quently went to the house of her sister, Mrs. Serah Jervis, in Water-street, and throwing a sovereign on the table said "cover that." The prisoner's husband, it was stated, had not worked for 12 months.—Evidence was given by Mrs. Mellon, Mrs. Jervis, and Jae. Miller Stnith.—lnspector Wood said the prisoner had been before the Bench on 32 previous occasions. She had been four times convicted of larceny, the lest occasion being seven years ago, when she was sentenced to nine months' hard labour.—The prisoner now pleaded guilty, and she was sentenced to three months' hard labour.

E Thompson, judge, at the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday fore- noon, David John Brooks, tailor, Widnes, brought an action to recover the sum of £1 14e 61 friarn James B. Aitken, chemical Manufacturer, Widnes, under emnewhat singular circumstances. The plaietiff was represented by Mr. H. L. Riley, of St. Helens, and Mr. Knowles, of Widnes, appeared for the defendant —lt was stated that some months ago a man named Hewitt entered the plaintiff's shop at Widnes and asked Brook to cash a cheque for £1 14s Gd, given by the defendant. Mr. Brooks cashed the cheque, but the cheque was never presented to the binkers, as Mr. Brooks last it a short time later. He spoke to the defendant about the matter, and he first protniaed him a new cheque, but afterwards refused to do so, or to repay the plaintiff the amount of the cheque.—Mr. Knowles said his client had offered to pay the plaintiff the amount of the cheque lost if the plaintiff would sign an indemnity note to refund the cash if the cheque was subsequently found. This the plain- tiff declined to do, and he (Mr. Knowles) was Instructed to ask for the costs that the defendant hod been put to by the plaintiff refusing to accept payment of the cheque in re- turn for an indemnity note.—His Honour remarked that the plaintiff had lost the cheque and then rushed into law with- out knowing his positiop, and thereby put himself and the defendant to expense. He gave judgment for the plaintiff for £1 14e 61 without costs, and made an order for the pay- ment of £1 as costs to the defendant. SMUGGLING AT RuNCoute.—Before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr, H Reynolds, at Runcorn Police Court, on Saturday, John Putt, master of the Screw steamer, Carron Park, of Glasgow, was charged with being unlawfully concerned in unsbipning certain goods liable to duty, such duty not be- ing paid and secured. Mary Elizabeth Putt, wife of the defendant, was charged with carrying away the goods with intent to defraud her Majesty of the duty.—The male de- fendant pleaded guilty and his wife not guilty. Mr. Samons, collector of customs, appeared to prosecute.—Thos. Garner, custonss officer, deposed that on Friday, the 15th inst., he was walking towards Weston Point, when he ob- served a boy wheeling some luggage towards the railway station. He ascertained that the luggage belonged to the captain of the Carron Park, and whilst standing near the defendants came up. He asked to be allowed to search the luggage, but the captain Paid there was nothing there but his wife's effects, and alleged that the officer was exceeding his duty by searching. He, however, made an examination and found five gills of perfumed spirits, six and three- quarter eill s of cordial, and 11b of tobacco upon which ne duty had been paid. He seized the goods and took the cap- tain prisoner. The captain said his wife had been a pas- senger on board the steamer, and when she was leaving he gave her the things he had purchased on the voyage, think- ing they were not of much value. He put the bottles and the tobacco into the luegage without his wife's knowledge. —The Bench considered there was no evidence against the wife and discharged her. The captain must, however, have known that he was doing wrong, and he would be tined £2 is 8d and costs 78. The Bench also ordered the spirits and tobacco to be forfeited.

CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, James Pemberton, herbal beverage manufacturer, Hilsbert-street, Simms Cross, was summoned for allowing a horse to be worked whilst in an unfit state, and Walter Pemberton, his son, was summoned for working the same,---P.S. McGregor deposed that about five o'clock on Monday, the nth inst., he saw the son driving a horse attached to a spring harry along Milton-road. The animal walked lame with one of its fore legs, and an examination revealed the fact that it was in poor condition, and suffer- ing from a raw wound the size of a florin under the collar. The wound was an old sore. The son teld the officer his father knew the state of the horse. He went to the father. who, when informed he would be reported, said, " There is not much wrong about it. You are short of a job if you report a thing like that." The officer considered it cruel to work the horse.—lnspector Wood stated that on the follow- ing day be examined the animal in the stable and found a lump about 24- inches in diameter on the near shoulder, and upon the top of this was a small wound about the size of a two shilling piece. The wound was covered with a slight I skin, and had been blacked. From the appearance the wound had been raw on the previous day. The animal was very lame on the fore leg, and was in low condition.. It was cruelty to work the horse. The boy denied that he had stated his father knew the condition of the horse, and the father contended that the horse was not in the bad stars described. He called a man named Edwardson, who said Pemberton. Sen., was ill at the time, and that 'be boy took the horse out on his own responsibility. The horse was right enough," 4nd fit to go out. There. was a little wound, a heat lump or something like that, upon the shoulder.—The case against the boy was withdrawn, as the Bench considered the father responsible, and fined him 19s and costs, 13s.

RCNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. A special meeting of this Board yeas held at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road, on Thursday morning, for the purpose of effiximt the seal of the Board to a memorial to the Mar- quis of Cholmondeley, asking him to take such steps as wonld preserve the Beacon Rock ; and also to affix the seal of the Board to a petition in Parli unent a,gainat the Man- chesttr Snip Cantl Bill. Mr. H. Shaw presided, and there were present Messrs. P. Speakman, J. Pritchtrd. W. Fisher, J. W. Lightburn, F. A. Lake, H. White, W. Whittaker S. , Taylor J. Williams, W. H. Linalier (law clerk), E. ;far- shall (sPcratarv), and M. Barker (surveyor.) BEACON ROCK : A If iIfORIAL TO LORD CHOLNONDELEY. The Stcrettry read the following memorial To the most lionouralie the Marquis of Cholmondeley. We, the . . . . .

Improvement Commissioners of the Town and District of Ruocorn, hereby respectfully memorialise your Lordship that you would in the exercise of your right as Lord cf the Manor, preserve the Beacon Rock on Runcorn Hill. We beg to draw your Lordship's attention to the prob,ble des- truction of the Rock, which is imminent in ceneequence of the extensive excavation of stone in the Qearry leased by Messrs. Goest and Son from your Lordship. We have received fvquent and forcible indications of the deep regret with which the threatened destruction of this historic and interesting landmark is viewed by the popula- tion of this town and district. One- of the grounds on which we make this appeal to your Lordship is that as the industries of this district in- crease, and the hitherto free and open spacee ae-erbed the populace telly appreciate the privilege afforded them of utilizing this eMvated rock from the summit of which an exceptionally floe view of wood, river, and mountain can be obtained. The attractiveness of the rock is r nhanced by the traditions and associations which surr nod it, one of which is commonly known te the people of Runcern, and frem which the rock takes its name, viz., that it formed one of the most con;p'cuous beacons of this district, and tradi- tion states that it woe frequenly used in the olden rime to warn the people of the country of the approach of an enemy. . May we advert to an inscription on the rock which shows incidentally that the attractiveness of the place has been appreciated for a long period of time, and the appropriate- ness of which is still verified by the residents. The in- *script ien is as fellows :—" This place is similar to Tuscalen and pleasant Tibur. Here when being wearied in the pur- suit ef knowledge, and worn out by the duties of my office, in this place I should desire a habitation in the time of old age. -Jur. Free, A.M., of Christ Church, Oxford, pro proctor of the University and Vicar of Runcorn, 1740." We trust that esour Lordship will generouely accede to our prayer that the Beacon Rack, on Runcorn Hill, may be preserved, repeating as tee do in this respect the earnest desire of the people of this town; and that the valued privilege so long accorded by your Lordship's ancestors may be coutinued t them."— The C: airman said it must be borne in mind that the Corn. miesioners had done up to the present all they possibly could in reference te this matter. The Board had no power to purchase any portion of Runcern Hill. For some months past they had been eneeavourme, thomigh the law clerk and a committee, to prevail upon the Marquis of Chelniondeley and Mr. Guest, to leave Beacon Rock undis- turbed. They bad not received that comtasy from those gentlemen that they were perhaps entitled to, and he thought the only step they could now take was to approach the Marquis by this memorial. They had hitherto ap- proeChed the agent without effect, and of course they would not be out of place in asking the Mrrquis to make soma, ar- rangement whereby nil concession might be orranted.— Mr. Speakmen propeeed that the seal of the Board be affixed to the memorial. They had had a promise from the late Marquis that he would keep Beacon Reck undisturbed, and he most earnestly hoped that the memorial to the present M arquie would have the effect desired try the moabitants of Runcern. If the rock was being removed for the purposes of cob:mercer then they should not have much to say, but it was simply a question of taking stone of very small value Irons under the hill, which would utterly destroy it. He therefore thought they were warranted in the course they were adopting that morning, which was quite in harmony with the wishes of the inheeitanta—ln answer to questions by Mr. Liehtburn, Mr. Speakman mid the statement he had m ide es ith respect to the late Marquis was in accordance with fact.--The Law Clerk said he had spoken to Mr. Bee- wick, the agent, and he then distinctly stated that he wOuld see the Marquis, and that the Marquis would no doubt pro- tect Beacon Hill. He hoped Mr. Besyick would eee the report of this Assertion, and his memory would thus be re- freshed.—Mr. Lake seconded the proposition. He said the Beard was always being pulled over the coils, and he thou 'lit it was advisable that the ratepae era should know clearly why they hid to adopt this course. The Marquis owned the minerals of the hill, and he bed leased the right to quarry those minerals to a townsman; and therefore, in the lace of such a contract, the Board could not put any pressure upon them. They could only go cap in hand and ask a favour, so there was no blame attaching to the Board for not p-ohicting, the hill, because it was not in their power to do so. He hoped the mernerial would be successful.—Mr. Lighthurn slid Mr. Guest did not look upon the rock with any poetic feeling. He did not associate himself with the lover's vows, the sage contem- plations, or the historical events associated with that bit of earth—he only locked upon it as producing so many cubie feet of stone, which was a natural view to teke. All the Hoard could say eves that they doplore the threatened de. struction exceedingly, and would do all in their power to preserve a prominent landmark of so much interest te the town. He saw Mr. Beswick the other day, and he was then very anxious to preserve the Beacon Rock, arid said he thought Mr. Guest would make an effort to spare the rock. —The resolution was carried unanimously.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
The monthly meeting was held on Thursday, Mr. T. S. Timmis presi.ing. Present—Messrs. Deacon, Imison, Shaw, Glover, and Danby (clerk).
PRIVATE ADVENTURE SCHOOLS.

The scheme `Ol-,iii-e'BiTt-rfc-i-Education Committee for the 1 periodical inspection of all private adventure schools in ' Whines, and the issuing of certificates when the results are satisfactory both as regards tho premises, teaching, disci- pline, and manner of keeping the registers, again came ut) for discussion. The cJrnpiete scheme was published a month ago.—Mr. Deacon, in movin4 the adoption of the scheme, said the committee had no desire to suppress those schools which were carrying on the work efficiently, but I they felt that it was necessary to have some scheme of the kind proposed to ascertain what work woe being done. The scheme was unanimously adopted by the committee.—ln reply 'o the chairman, Mr. Deacon said the question was whether they should appoint some gantleman from Liver- pool, where the duties wert generally performed by clergy- men at so much for each inspection, t) carry out the inspec- tion, or whether some gentleman in the neighbourhood capable of performing the work should be appointed.—The Chairman said the way in which the gentlemen of the Com- mittee had conducted the most arduous duties entrusted to them should be a sufficient guarantee that they would not use these powers in an arbitrary manner. They could not suppress any school without the fiat of the magistrates, and he thought the schema should e adopted.—The reso- lution was carried.

div.head: DE AF AND Dunn CHILDREN.
div.p: DE AF AND Dunn CHILDREN.

Mr. Deacon stated that the District Education Committee bad made arrangements with the Prescit Board of Guar- dians for the El even or twelve deaf, dumb, and blind chil- dren in Widnes, which hitherto had not been in attendance at any Behead., to be sent to 9nitable institutions where they would be prewtly educated. The parents had been con- sulted, and with the exception of one or two had expreesed their willingness to pay the snot proposed by the Guar- dians.—The Chairman said this report was very s atis- factory.

div.head: DISTRICT EDUCSTION COMMITTEE.
div.p: DISTRICT EDUCSTION COMMITTEE.

Tbis committee reported that during the month of April there were 224 applications for school fees, and 259 persons appeared before the onnmittee for contravention of the Educatioo Act. Fee were recommended tlhe piid in 207 cases, ant 42 persons were prosecuted before the magistrates, 40 being convicted.

div.p: THE 8111 P CANAL 6C anti.

The Chairman said with referenc; to fi.111147, the seal of the Board to a petition to the Efsuse of Commons against the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, the committee had in- tended to state the exact position in which they stood with regtrd to the promoters of the bill, but the committee had to meet the promoters next day, and it would not be policy on the part of the Board to enter into any discussion with reference to the matter. All the committee were seeking at the present time was to put themselves in a proper position to carry out the wishes of the Board as given to them up to this time, and they did not think it advisable that that meeting should do anything further than merely to pass the resolution. Then when they had got RS they could come to an arrangement with the promoters, they would lay the whole facts before the Board, so that they would know exactly how they stood.—Mr Pritchard moved that the seal of the Board be affixed to the pet tion.—Mr. Lightbarn ecconded.—Mr. Lake said he should be sorry te do anything which might interfere with the negotiations which were going on, but it seemed to him that asking them to pass that resolution without discussion was like tying their hands and fighting afterwards. There wee very little use in a discussion as to the course the com- mittee had adopted in the past, and whether they ought to be trusted in the future if the Board had already given them full powers. The committee had opposed the bill in the House of Lords, and now they asked the Board to do the same thing in the House of Commons. He thought the members ought to have some good reasons shown them that they would be more saccessfnl in one Renee than Has other. Otherwise it was only throwing good money after had.—The Law Clerk : The course we took in the House of Lords was . taken nyder the advice of the c mosel. The Chairmen : Is not this a proper answer. If you don't succeed in getting what you want in one House you should proceed to the other.—Mr. Lake: If you have any clones of succeeding.—The Chairman : Exactly. Mr. Lake : I ask if you have any reasonable hope of success.— The Chairman : The committee do not say they have been unsuccessful. They would differ with you as to what they have done.—Mr. Lake: Exactly. We have iao report, and yet you ask us for further powere—The Chair-

.. - . man : e are only continuing in the same course that the Board said we must proceed with. This is no new depar- ture.—Mr. Lake: It is not an entirely new departure.—The Chairman: It is a mere formality.—Mr. Lake: And a very exprisice one, too. If you had succeeded in one house von need not have gene to the other. My i ojectionwas as to the mode in which the opposition was conducted n the Upper House.—The Chairman again repeated that discuesion would not be far the advantage of the town. If they liked they could resolve the Board into a committee.—Mr. Lake: That Ido not see the necessity for. I have no desire to keep anything back I have to say from the public—Mr . Pritchard expressed the opinion that discussion would not be for the public good. and Mr. Lake said under the circum- stances he would reserve anything he had to say until a later day.—After a little further discussion, the resolution was passed nem con—lt was left to the discretion of the Chairman of the Committee as to whether a special meeting was held to discuss the question.

OYsinostftwo.--7Michael Walsh was charged with ill- treating a horse on the 14th bat by over-loading it. P.C. Neil was near the poliaS "office; when he saw defendant driving a horse and lorry. The luny was laden with long iron, which was dragging-a distance of six or seven feet on the ground. The horse had great difficulty in drag- ging its lead up Church-street. Subsequent enquiries showed that COI/load was a very heavy one, the total weight being 4 tone 7 cwt.—Defendant said that the lorry was not a suitable one, and the iron shifted, making the load difficult to draw. DEAR FRBD,—Tos will -b. surprised at receiving is lettse hem me. but thank God. I am pleased ti-say 412 getting 'better every day. I *bag be so glad to ' breathe the frekh air again It has seemed $ dreadral Icing time to be in bed. Too know I was taken to be Hosoleal last April to be treated for Bright's Disease of the Kidneys. Well, on the 31s1 of July they tapped me, and took away 301 ounaes of water. The same thing was done again on the 18th September, and aell imams of water obtained. On the 9th October I was discharged from the Hospital as incurable. In Jesu- itry this year (the 20th), was again tapped at home and 3.30 ounces of water taken away. The St. Bar- tholomew's Hospital in London refused me admissime as a hopeless case, and the St. Barthelensew'sH•tpitai. Chatham. also refused me, as being the worst case troy hart seen for years, and two local doctors gave me up M hopeless. When I came from the Hoapial It to ,k three to put use to bed. My clothes had to be Out off I was an object of misery and despair. After the Hospitals had refused me and doctors gives me up. my wife persuaded me to try Hop Bitters, aid from be commencement have improved tally. I have only takers them seven weeks and can now get down- stairs sad walk about without even a stick. With the aid f a few mo-e bottles of the Bitters shall be well again. The water has entirely left my body and legs. , The only trace left is in my feet. It is a wonderful aseetio'ne. I wish I bad tried it sooner, as I have nearly ruined myself and family with lectors' bills and other expenses. I might have been well long ago. At the Hospital I had no appetite whatever, but slam usiag the Bitters eat everything with a relish. The oily difilantty is th s expense, but must not mind that so long as lam getting well. Am cheerful now that recovery is near, fir everyone had given me up as a bad job. With best wishes to I remain, your affect onate Brother, (Sigrisi) William °reptile. • I, Bush Terrace, Cage Lane, Chatham, March 14, 1884. To the Hop Dittos- s Co., Londm. NOTES BY ThU WAY. The match Lancashire v. Nineteen Colts of Ashton. under. Lyne was net resumed on Saturday until bait-past one, owing to the heavy rain that had fallen since the previous day's play, and at six o'clock the game was drawn in favour et the eleven.—At Nottingham, on Saturday, the Sussex team failed to follow up their performances against Notts. of the two previous days, and Notts. gained a deci- sive victory by nine vricketel. The totals were, Sussex 201 and 80; Notts. 167 and 115 with nine wickets to spare. In the second innings of the winning team Gunn made 63 1 and Scotton carried out his bat with 39 to his credit. Flowers made 54 for Notts., and for Sussex Hide and Hum• phreye made the highest inclividnal scores.—The match Ox- ford Eleven v. next Sixteen was resumed at Oxford on Saturday, the result proving an easy win for the next Six- teen by toi wickets, while at Cambridge the game between First Twelve and next Sixteen was drawn. At Lord's, on Tuesday, Kent gained an easy victory over the Merleybone club by six wickets. After the advantage the County gained on Monday, the result is not surprising, and tke better side evidently won. For Marleybone, liornby and Scotton put on 56 for the first wicket, and Hornby, while he was in, made 84 out of 105. The Lancashire captain ',lade some splendid hits, including six 4's, seven 3's, and thirteen 2's.

When play ceased in the Cambridge University v. an Eleven of England match, on Tuesday, England had com- pleted their first innings for 235 and made 165 in their second venture for nine wickets, whilst Cambridge had scored 231 in their first inniogs. The game was to have been resumed c n Wednesday, .but ow- ing to heavy rain the match was abandoned.— ' Rain fell heavily at Bradford on Tuesday night and Wed- nesday morning, and at one o'clock, as the weather showed no signs of improvement, it was decided to abandon the match Yorkshire v. Sussex, the score on Tuesday night beink :—Yorkshire, 377; Sussex, 105.—From an early hour on Wednesday morning rain fell heavily at Oxford, and there being no signs of abatement at three o'clock the match between Oxford University and M.C.C. and Ground was abandoned. The score on Tuesday night was :—Mary- leLone, first innings, 244 ; second innings, 178 for five wickets. Oxford, firet innings, 108.

NEW RATES.—Oa the application of Mr. Ilmighton, amis. tent overseer, the magistrates at the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday signed a new poor rate of 2s in the £ for Bold, and eid in the # for Crouton. A LOCOMOTIVE ON THE HIGHWAY.—Before Mr. W. ?if- kington and Lieutenant-Colonel W. W. Pilkington, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Albert Smith, an engine driver, residing at Great Crosby, was summoned for unlaw- fully driving a locomotive on the highway (Derby-street, Present) after sunset and before midnight on the 7th inst. The defendant, who pleaded guilty, said his engine was short of water, and le could not get along as quick as be otherwise would have done.—The Bench ordered him to pay the costs.

AN ACCIDENT.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tues- day, Joseph Skinner, a butcher at Liverpool, was summoned for obstructing the highway at Buyton on the sth March.— The defendant pleaded guilty.--P.C, Crooks stated that about midnight on the date named he found a cart, one wheel of which was in a ditch, and the shafts reachin&al most across the road, in Whiston-lane, Buyton. The shafts were in a dangerous position for any approaching horses and traps, and witness with great difficulty put them in a eater posi- tion. The cart was net removed until the afternoon of the following day. The defendant said that when he was going up the " brow " his horse suddenly backed, and the cart was pushed into the ditch. He tried to get assistance to remove the cart, but failed to do so. The spring of the cart was also smashed. On the suggestion of the Benet] Superintendent Barker withdrew the summons. SNociturci NnoLacr or FAMlLY.—Before Messrs. W. Pilkington and W. W. Pilkington, at tlle Preiscot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Dennis Kehoe, described as a chemi- cal labourer, of Widnes, was charged under a warrant with deserting his wife and family, whereby they became charge- able to the Present Union.—Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Board of Guardians, prosecuted, and stated that the pri- soner's wife and six children became chargeable to the Free- cot Union on the 26th April. Prior to the deeertion the prisoner was in constant employment at Messrs. Pilkingtons' Chemical Works, Widnes, and was in receipt of good wages. For some reason unknown to the Guardians the prisoner left the district and he was apprehended in Dublin on Saint- day last. The prisoner left his family in a pitiable plight, with not a bed to lie upon, and the children were almost naked, He asked the Bench to inflict the full penalty, as it was not the first time the prisoner had left his family.—Mr. Scannel, relieving officer, gave evidence to the foregoing effect, after which the Bench sentenced the prisoner to ens month's imprisonment with bard labour.

A PRIIISCOT DITOECH Cat:la.—ln the Divorce Court, on Monday, Sir James Mennen and a jury bad before them the suit of Johnson v. Johnson and Charles Darley. This was a petition by Johnson, a retired non-csnomiesioned offi- cer, living at Preacot, for a divorce on the ground of his wife's adultery with the es-respondent, a solicitor, 0 Black- burn, against whom damages were claimed. Tnere was no defence to the action. According to the evideace the parties were married In June, 1883, the so-respondent being at the wedding breakfast, and making them a pre- sent. Subsequently petitioner thought the eo-reepondent ' visited his house too frequently, and complained to his wife of her apparent intimacy with the e,o-respondeat. She then, to his surprise, admitted that improper relations had existet between them both before and after her mar- riage. Petitioner thereupon caused inquiries to be made, and ascertained that upon occasions when he visited Black- burn with his wife—and she slept at the house of her father, and he at the residence of his mother—she availed herself of the opportunity of going to the co-reapondent's offices, where she remained until a late hour.—The jury, after a abort deliberation, assessed the damages at £250, which were ordered to be paid into court, and a decree nisi was pro- nounced. SamOt's CITARGA AGIIN9r • PIODBALIR.—Thontas Lew*, a pigdealer at Rainhill, was summoned at the Prescot Petty Sessions, before Messrs. W. Pilkingten and W. W. Pilkisg- ton, on Tu.sday, for failing to report swine fever to the police authorities. The defendant pleaded not guilty.— Superintendent Barker stated that the defendant resided at Fishpond House, Rainhill, and seld pigs at various markets. He visited the defendant's house on the 3rd May, in corn- piny with Mr. Weleby, veterinary surgeon, and they found four pigs lathe cote, one of which was suffering from swine fever. The defendant had given no information of the dis- ease. They afterwards visited the farm of Mr. Roberts, who had nurc'meedtwo pigs from the defendant, and found them also suffering from swine fever. Mr. It)berts ex- changed the pigs for two others, which were also found to be suffering from the same disease. He had six infected areas in his district caused by the defendant selling pigs.— Mr. Welsby gave evidence in support of Superintendent Barker's statement, and added that be had made a post, mortem examination of one of the pigs, and it was one of the worst cases he had ever seen.—Superintendent Barker stated that the defendant had been previously convicted for a similar offence, but he appeared to take no notice of the Act. That CaSe was one of the worst cases be bad known of wilfully evading the Act.—The Beech : We fine you 120 and costa, £1 e Sd.

TIM EDUCATION OF WORKING-CLASS CHILDREN.—Mr. Mundells, speaking in London, on Saturday, said that what- ever happened to the middle classes of the country the children of the working classes would get a sound elemen- tary education. The elementary teacher should have a better training, and a larger and a more liberal education than he bad received up to the present- he should come more into contict with University men, and he should ob- tain son-is of the advantages which the universities of this country and of Bcotiand could afford for the services of the teacher.

LORD SALISBURY ON THB GOTHRNICHNT.—Lord Salisbury was present on Wednesday night at the annual dinner of the Middlesex Conservative Association at Knightsbridge. In responding to the toast of "The Conservative party," he protested against Lord Granville's attempt to limit the scope of public discussion on the Government policy. He held that now, when the independence of the Hones of Commons was gone, free discussion in putilic meeting be- came of supreme importance. He could not accept Lord Granville' s limitations He could not describe a surrender as anything but a surrender. He had come to the conchs- Sion that the worst chapters in the maladministration of the Government were due to the want of sustaining impulse to I drive them forward on the path on which they once entered. This was illustrated in the abandonment of the Soudan cam- ;moque,. and he feared that it would be again illustrated on the Afghan frontier. He considered the Russian Govern- ment to be actuated by two impulses—one inducing them to give assurances, and the other the imperative necessity which caused their continuous advance towards India. That advance could only be stopped by England'a reliance , on bear own right arm.

The enthronisatien of Dr. King as Bishop of Lincoln took place on Wednesday morning. RIOTING.—At Airdrie, on Tuesday, seventeen men were convicted of rioting at BeHebei!, on Saturday, and were each sentenced to 60 days' imprisonment. OR Tuesday morning, a the broke out at Mr. Jar. Togg's cotton spinning mill, Bolton. The damage amounts to £lO,OOO, fully covered by insurance. The new Old Testament is a great commercial success for the publishers. Scarcely a day and a half had elapsed from the issue of the first edition before a second was ordered.
A. letter from Lord Wolseley to the Goyerner•General of Canada is issued among Parli,tmentary papers of Thursday testifying to the competency and skill and courage of the Canadian voyageur*. "

At a confe'rencs of miners' delegates held at Barnsley, on Thursday, it was resolved to continue the strike which has now been going on for several weeks in resistance to the masters' proposal to reduce wages. A man-of-war built for the Japanese Government, lamed the Takachiho Kan, was launched on the Tyne on Satur- day. 'The vessel is described to be one of the swiftest and most heavily armed cruisers in existence. At Hull, on luesday, Joha Kelly, sailor, was committed for trial on a coroner's warrant, charged with the man- slaughter of a man named Ward in a house of ill-fame. The prisoner shot deceased with a revolver during a quarrel.

At the Old Bailey, on Thursday, Charles Morgan, 44, pleaded gulty to falsifying accounts and stealing seouri- ties of the value of £lO,OOO while manager of a stock- broking business, and he was sentenced to ten years' penal servitude. A FATAL Svaan.-00 Monday two men were found help- lessly drunk on the highway at Cern, Ruabon, with a bottle of whisky at their side. A raedical examination soon proved that one was dead and that the other was in a very serious state.

Exaonnow OF JAMBS Les —On Monday morning. Jac Lee, convicted of the murder of Police•lnepector Sim- mons, was executed at Chelmsford Gaol. His last words were. "I die innocent." His wife had her last interview with him on Saturday. A WINDHILL FIRIIII DT LIGHTNING —A heavy thunder- storm passed over Dover on Sunday. Six sheep 'tenting by a wire !.ace, were killed by lightning ; a large tree was struck and cat down several feet, while a windmill at Woot- ton was set on fire and burnt to the ground. At Oldham, on Wednesday, John Taylor was again re- mended on a charge of attempting to kill by shooting a gentleman named William Whittaker; with whom the prisoner bad a dispute as to regally matters. The chief con- stable said Mr. Whittaker was only slightly better. Tau ILLNISS ow Vforou 11000.—The Paris correspond- ent of the Exchange Company telegraphs that on inquiry at eight o'clock on Thursday morning he was informed that M. Victor Hugo had pasaed a relatively good night, but his condition is unchanged, and a fatal Issue of his illness may occur at any moment.

The Prince of Wales on Thursday inspected the Norfolk Artillery Militia, at Yarmouth, in the presence of several thousands of spectators. His Royal Hichness at the close somplimented the brigade on their etnadiness, smartness, and discipline, and said he was proud to know that his son btlonged to the regiment. In the Queen's Bench Division' on Thursday, a new trial was moved for in the action of Maskelyne v. Bishop, on the ground of surprise, and that the damages were excessive. Mr. Justice Field said that £lO,OOO damages were far too much, and he directed that the damages should go back to the court below for reassessment. IitOTAL VISIT TO PRBSTON.—At a special meeting of the Preston Town Council, on Wednesday, the Mayor an- nounced that the ?dice of Wales would visit the Royal Agricultural Show at Preston on the 6th July and suc- ceeding day. Trrais.—A bill was issued on Saturday for extending to parishes in England and Wales, in whioh the tithe rent. charge is payable under Enclosure Acts and souse other local Acts, the same permissive facilities for commuting tithes which are granted to other parishes. The parishes te which this bill seeks to ex;end these facilities are about 400 in number.

A GEINBROI7II LANDLORD.—Captain Congreve, of Burton, near Chester, has returned to all his tenants the handsome sum of 23 per cent on their rents in cmsideration of the agricultural depression, which is still keenly felt in the arable districts of the county. The dairy farmers of Cheshire have, however, experienced two fairly prosperous seasons in succession.

TIES COURT.—The Queen and Princess Beatrice left Windsor Castle on Thursday night for Balmoral. Her Majesty has written to the Archbishop of Canterbury thanking the Primate and Convocation of Cmterbury for their presentation copy of the revised scriptures, and Isom- gratulating the revisers on the successful manner in which they hare accomplished their undertaking.
