MIIRDRR.—The adjourned coroner's in- quest on the body of a male child aged two years, who was found drowned on Sunday last in a brook near Clitheroe, , was held at Slaitlburn on Tnursday. The jury returned, a verdict of wilful murder agtinst Graze Isherwood, wife of a farmer, and her sister, Isabella Gardner, both of whom are ' in custody. The deceased was the illegitimate eon of the first-named woman,

ADAMS V. COISRIDGE.—In the. Conrt of Appeal on Thurs- day, Mr. Adams, the plaintiff in the case of Adams v. Coleridge, applied to have a day fixed for the hearing of his appeal against the judgment a Mr. Justice Maniety setting aside the verdict of the jury for £3,000. The Master of the Rollo said the appeal could not be heard until after Whit. suntide holidays, Mr. Adams pressed for an early day, and the Master of the Rolls said Thursday, 4th June, would be fixed if the day suited both sides. - MANCHESTER BErrixo, auss.—The persons apprehended by the Manchester police during their raid on betting clubs on Wednesday were taken before the Stipendiary and other magistrates on Thursday, and remanded. It is stated that nearly £3,000 was found npon the prisoners. Reference to the action of the authorities was madeat the anrual meet. lng of the Working Men's Clubs Association, on Thursday, by the Mayor and Dean of Manchester. The Dean expres. a very strong hope that action Of this kind would not be confined to clubs frequented by men of any one class, but that the authorities would turn their attention to what might be ealled the higher clams.

Tan 6v. /Iguana AND WIGAN JUNCTION RAILWAY.—The bill for the promotion of this line was read for the third time in the House of Common' on Tuesday night, and passed. GOOD TEMPLARY.—The weekly session of the Rope of Earleetown Lodge of Good Templars was held on Mon- day evening, when Bro. George Clarke, W.C.T., presided. Arrangements were made for paying a visit to the Great Heart Lodge, St. Helene, 02 the evening of the following day. Linens/. lacrunna.—The Executive Committee of the Liberal '300" for the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire have arranged for a series of lectures by the Rev. D. S. Prosser, of Walkden. On Friday evening the first on " Why should working-men be Liberals ?" will be delivered at Golberne, and on Monday the same lecture will be given at Rainhill. On Thursday next, at Ashton, the Rev. D. S. Prosser will lecture on "The present Government —a vindication."

NEWTON Fem.—The annual "May fair" was held at Newton on Monday. The weather being very favourable the fair was well patronised by the farmers of the surrounding townships. As on former occasions High- street, " the only street in Newton," was almost entirely blocked with cattle, horses, &c., while a number of shooting galleries, gingerbread and toffee stalls were erected opposite the Town Hall and St. Peter's Church. It was estimated that about 200 head of cattle were offered for sale, and a considerable number were disposed of. The horses num- bered about 300, and the majority changed owners. The quality of both cattle and horses was fair and up to the average. In the evening there was a very large attendance lof people, the proprietors of the shooting galleries, dm., doing a "roaring trade." BOWLING.—Park Hotel Bowling Club v. Earlestown Reereation.—Thesa clubs bowled their return match en Saturday, on the Park Hotel Bowling Green, Park-lane. The green was in splendid condition, and some good play was shown, Earlestown being victorious on both greens, by 311 on Earlestown Green and 17 on the Park Hotel Green, making a total of 50 in both matches. After the bowling all sat down to a tea provided by Mrs. Canllffe. Mr. Finch, sub-captain to the visitors, was called to the chair, and Mr H. Lowe, captain of the home team, to the vice. chair. HELENS.—OR Tuesday evening upwards of 25 members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Tempters proceeded to pay a fraternal visit to the "Great Heart " Lodge, St. Helens. The visitors arrived at the Templars' Hall, George-street, about 7-45 p.m. and were invite] to occupy the officers' chairs, Bro. George Clarke, P.W.D.31 , presiding. After the admission of a candidate the Lodge was opened to friends, when a number attended, the room being nicely filled. The Chairman gave a short address, after which a programme was gone through in a highly creditable manner. Songs were given by Bro. John Taylor and &eters E. Whitley, E. Clarke, and E. Smith, and a duett nicely rendered by Sisters M. E. and E. Clarke. Appropriate recitations were well delivered by Bros. J. Warburton and G. E. Warburton and Sister C. E. Barnard ; and capital readings were given by Bros. E. Newman' and James Barnard. The Lodge Choir also tendered several glees and melodies very satisfactorily. At the conclusion of the programme Bro. J. Brockbank, in a few remarks, moved a vote of thanks to the visitors for their excellent entertainment, which was seconded by Bro. J. Bird, who expressed a hope that the return visit might I only be as successful. Bro. G. Warburton, senr., responded, latter which the meeting closed, when the visitors sat down 'to an excellent repast, kindly provided by the St. Helene friends. The Earlestown friends returned home by train at 10-20 p.m., having thoroughly enjoyed their visit. Tan LANCASHIRE HUSSARS AT SOOTHPOIIII. The Lancashire Hussars Yeomanry Cavalry are this week un- dergoing their annual week's training and drill at South- port. The "C " (Newton) troop, numbering about 50 men, under Adjutant Moreland, left Newton about seven o'clock on Monday morning and marched to Ashton, where they joined the "A" (Ashton-in-Makerfield) troop., along with the band. The two troops proceeded to Rainford, where they found the " B" (Moss Bank) troop awaiting them, and at Ormakirk the "D " (Grmskirk) troop joined them. The regiment then proceeded to Southport, where they arrived in the afternoon. On Monday. Tuesday. and Wednesday the men were put throogh drilla and various movements, and on Thursday and Friday the horse and sword competitions were held. The anneal inspection will take place to-day (Saturday), the inspeeting officer being Lord C. Kerr. On Sunday the moo will attend Holy Trinity Church, Southport,and start for home on Monday morning. The sword competition look place on Thursday, In the Skating Hall at the Winter Gardens, the judge beiog leaclog-Inspector Dixon of the sth Dragoon Guards, sta- tioned at Manchester. The following was the result :-1 Troop (Ashton-in-Makerfield): First prize, Private Mtta ; second, Sergeant Glover; third, Sergeant Shaw. 11 Troop (St. Helens, Wigan, and neighbourhood) : First, Private W. Littler ' • second, Corporal Sephton ; third, Corporal Sum- ner. C Troop (Newton and Liverpool) : First, Corporal Gilbert ; second, Farrier-Sergeant Ritchie ; third, Private Naylor. D Troop (Ormekirk and Lathorn) : First, Private Wells; second, Private Joseph Cave; third, Corporal Spencer. The regimental prize was wont after a severe competition, by Private W. I ittler of .13- Troop.

div.head: EARLESTOWN FOOTBALL CLUB,
div.p: EARLESTOWN FOOTBALL CLUB,
CONCERT LIM PRESENTATLONS.

One of the most enthusiastic gatherings ever held. in Earlestown took place on Monday evening, when the fifth annual concert in connection with the Earlestown Football Club WS, bold in the Viaduct Institute. The popularity of the gathering was in a great measure due to the announce- ment that the splendid trophy known m the Liverpool and District Challenge Cup, and the handsome gold medale, won by the Earleetown Club, would be publicly presented to the winning team by the President of the dab, Mr. Thomas Stone, of Newton Park. Though the final tie of the Challenge Cup Competition, when Earlestowa defeated the then cop-holders, Everton, by one goal te none, was played ever two months ago, the cup and medals were only handed over to the representatives of the Earlestown Club a fort- night ago. Since then they had been in the custody of Mr. Thomas Stone (president) at his residence, and had not been publicly exhibited in the district. Prior to the con- cert on Monday evening, the Earlestown players were con- veyed in a waggonette to Newton Park, the residence of their esteemed President. WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB. ANNUAL DINNER. The ann dal dinner in connection with this flourishing Club was held at the Railway Inn, Victoria.road, Widnes, on Wednesday evening, when an excellent meal was placed on the tables by the host and hostess, Mr. and Mrs. Anderson. Pall juetice was done to the repast by a company of about I,ixty persons. At the subsequent meeting the chair was occupied by Dr. McCambridge, and amongst those also pre- Sent were Dr. O'Carroll, Messrs. H. 0. Richards, T. Smith, W. Oakden, R. Herriman, Melvin, W. Holt, A. M. Harrison, W. Ireland, C. Hemingway, J. Ashen, F. T. Simcock, F. Plampton, &c.—The Cnai:man proposed the " Queen," neaten was enthusiastic ally received—Mr. Ireland, in pro- posing the "Guest ot the evening," explained that unfor- tanately that vutleman was not present. lie referred to Mr. Lim Briggs, who had just returned from Australia. The committee had thought it well to combine with their Annual dinner the opportunity of welcoming Mr. Briggs on his return, as one who bad on past occasions identified him- self with them. That night they did not purpose to receg- Übe him exactly as a football player, but they wished to I Show their appreciation of his perfortnancesin Australia in the cricketang line. (Applause.) Mr. Briggs was anxious to be present, but was called upon to represent his comity against Oxford University, and, as the game commenced the next morning, he could not possibly be present. He did not think he need refer minutely to the performances abroad of Mr. Briggs, as he had no doubt every one present had followed them v-ry zlosely. He might say, however, that Mr Briggs had, he thought, ex- ceeded the most sanguine expectations, as the recently pub- lished results would show. (Applause.) He believed Mr. Briggs was third on the list of batting aa err !,es, a Position for c 0 young a cricketer. They had not him present, but they had a worthy substitute in his father, and he should a=lt them without more ado to drink to the health of "Jack" Briggs.—The toast was acknewlennea with musical honours and ringing cheers, and n r. James Briggs, in returning thanks, vouched for the fact that 1. JAck " was very sorry he could not be present.—Mr. Pansy gave " The Widnes Football Club." It had, he said, secured a reputa- tion which was well sustained by the present members. That was evidenced by the results of the past season, and, no doubt, so long as the club was composed of members like it now possessed, its reputation was secure. (Applause.)— Nr. A. Brown respan eel in appropriale terms —Mr. Oakden propesed the health of the " Presidents and vice-presidents." As these gentlemen were well known to (Joe members of the club, he need nat recapitulate their good qualities. All knew that they were men of the right sort. (Cheers.) In these days, when so many croakers depreciated football and manly gaines, they should be gratified that they had such gentlemen at their head. He did not think they could have a more worthy preiident than Mr. E. Deacon, and he did not think any club in the country had better vice-presidents. Tho toast, which was very cordially honoured, was acknow- ledged by the Chairman, one of the vice-presidents.— alr. Ashall, in proposing the visitors, gave them a hearty wel- come. Incidentally, he mentioned that he should be happy to receive the names of any new members for next season, and that it was intended to pay fares both ways, provided, Of coarse, that they rec,ived sufficient funds. With the toast he coupled the name of Mr. Holt, who acknowledged the compliment.—The health of the " Press " was proposed by Mr. Richards, And acknowledged by Mr. S. Harrison, of The Exarniner.—Daring the evening songs of all-round ex- cellence were given by Dr. O'Carroll, the Chairmen, and Messrs. Kiddie, Holt, Ireland, Harrison, Leach, Farrell, Bar- ton, Simcock, and otners, and the meeting passed off very pleasantly.

MR. T. P. O'CONNOR, M.P., AT WIDNES. Ihe Widnes branch of the Irish National League of Great Britain was inaugurated on Wednesday eveniog Or a public meeting held in the Volunteer Hall. Mr. T. P. O'Connor, M.P. for Galway, had promised to be present to deliver an address, and during the afternoon he was driven from Warrington in a carriage drawn by a pair of greys. He was accompanied by Dr. O'Keeffa (Widnes), Mr. W. F. Cox (Manchester), Mr. Martin Cox (London), and Messrs. Quinn, Fitzpatrick, and S. Faulkner (Widnes). At Halton View the local band of the League, attired in their bright green uniform, met the party and escorted them t.) Been. don Horise, the residence of Dr. O'Keeffe, where they were entertained until the time of meeting. They then proceeded to the Vciunteer Hall accompanied by the baud, a large number of persons having assembled in the thoroughfare to see the hon. gentleman, whom they accorded a hearty re- ception. Dr. O'Keeffe was voted to the chair, and ia addi- tion te ths gentemen previously mentioned, he was sup- ported on the platform by Messrs. M‘Kinley (St. Helens), 1 Conway (Blackburn), F. Loughlin (Widnes), B. Fox, Lalor,l O'Malley, and O'Donoghue (Liverpool), and Ryan (Whines). Although the lowest charge for admission was pi, the hall was at least three parts filled, amongst the audi- ence being many English Liberals. The Chairman, who was greeted with cheering, said as they were aware a branch of the Irish National League of Great Britain had been recently and su idenly established in Widnes for the purpose of causing all Irishmen who resided there to be able to present a united front on any platform. and also in order to prepare them to make proper , use of the powers that the new franchise would give them when it became the law of the land. (Hear, hear.) In the Widnes division of South-West Lancashire there was an enormous population of Irishmen, and every householder Would be entitled to a Parliamentary vote at the next general election, which would probably take place in a few months. (A voice : "The sooner and the better.") It was absolutely necessary that an organisation should be formed that would enable them to place every Irish householder on the register. (Cheers.) It was some years since they had the honour of having a member of Parliament to address them in Widnes. They had a few candidates for Parlia- ment honours a few years ago, but they were net M.P.'s then, and they cared very little about them after they became M.P.'s. (Hooting.) But now a member of Parlia- ment who stood more than six feet high—(applause)— would address them that night, and would tell the Irish people in what manner they ought to vote. He congratu- lated them that at that meeting in connection with the , Irish Nationalists they were not subject to the surveillance or espionage of the police, as were their friends at Warring- ton. (Cheers.) Fortunately Inspector Wood, the officer in Command at Widnes, was both liked by his own men—and that was one of the highest recommendations that an officer of the police could have—and was also liked by the public. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) The inspector knew that the people of Widnes were able to conduct themselves in such an exceilzet meener that there was no occasion for the in- troduction of detectives amongst them at a meeting, or for the abominable espionage, which was so detestable in itself, and so hateful to any person of refined feelings. ("Loud cheers.) Mr. Loughlin moved the following resolution :—" That we, the members of the Widnes Branch et the Irish National League, beg to record oar unabated confidence in Mr. C. S. Parnell and his party in their efforts to obtain for Ireland her legielative independence; and we pledge ourselves to use all lawful and constitutional means to support them in those efforts." (Cheers.) Owing, he said, to the able ad- vocacy of Mr. Parnell and his party, the Irish cause had prospered and sprung by leaps and bounds during the last five or six years more than it had done for the previous 80 years. (Cheers.) The resolution had his entire sympathy, and he was confident the sympathy of that vast assembly in common with Irishmen all the world over. (Cheers.) Mr. Fee ,econded the resolution, which was carried enthusiastically. Mr. T. P. O'Connor, M.P., on rising to reply, was greeted with an ovation, the audience rising to their feet en masse. He said he must make the confession that he was not only delighted, but to a considerable extent surprised, by the enthusiasm and magnitude of the reception which be had eeceived that day from the Irishmen of Widnes—(cheers)— end from that time forward be thought he might promise theta that the spell of silence which had hung over the town for No many years was entirely broken, and that Widnes would receive from the leaders of the Irish movement that amount of attention' which the strength of the Irish popule den within the town, and the heartiness and earnestness, and the patriotism amongst them so highly deserved at their hands. (Cheers.) It had been argued that the inhabitants of vari- ous parts of Ireland were opposed to each other. Since the Franchise and the Redistribution Acts had passed this had been convincingly proved to be an error, and not only Ire- land, but the whole world knew, and would know better after the next general election—(cheers arid laughter)— that the province of Ulster was like the province of Con. naught, Leinster, or Munster—that was to say, that the . overwhelming majority of its people were determined that Ireland should regain her national rights. (Loud cheers.) There had not been a period in Irish history when the heart of the people had not been som,d, but the representation of the people had been rotten, In every election a majority of members were re- turned who went to Parliament either for the purpose of backing up the infamy of the landlords or selling themselves to the highest bidder on either side of the House. (Hoot- ing.) The cause of this was, owing to the restriction of the franchise, that the majority of the people hal no real voice in the selection of their representatives. But that time was past; the reign of small constituencies was ended ; the regime of cliques and corruption was passed, and Irish liberty now stood upon the broad and iniffstruc- tibia basis of the people, all entitled to share in the repre- sentation. (Loud cheers.) }Warring to the preerroes the netionel party hid m ade in Parliament since 1880, when they were small and weak, up to the present time, the speaker said they were determined to be always in opposi- tion to any Enelieh ministry until the rights of Ireland were restored. (Cheers) They saw the result. A coercion bill was formerly a matter of course for Leland, but now it was a thing of which nearly every Englishman was heartily aehamed, and he never saw Mr. Gladstone so humil- iated, so ashamed, and so nervoas as he was a few nights ago, when he announced the shameful resolve of the Government to bring in a new coercion bill for Ireland. (Hooting.) eafbedy could say there was any crime in Ireland at the present moment. There was only one crime, and that was the Lich nation hated, teethed, and detested Lord Spencar and Dublin Castle. (Loud groans.) The announcement in the evening papers that Mr. Glad- stone had promised to improve the purchase clauses of the Land Act of 1881 was another evidence of the power of the Irish people. Thev had brought things to such a pass in Ireland that the landlord was more anxious for settlement than the tenant; that the tenant could afford to wait, know- ing th' t time and the seasons and resistless forces were 011 his side, whilst tha landlord was face to face with impending bankruptcy, and begging the 5f ate to ctne to his aid. (Lou! cheers The Irish people would not be satisii•el with any Laud Act which did not make the tenant, the tiller of the aoieehe owner of the land witnout any landlord over him except the

THE NEW PUBLIC OFFICES FOR WIONES. At the offices of the Local Board, Alforde Chambers, on Thursday, Major Tullocb, inspector to the Local Govern- ment Board, held a public inquiry respecting the applica- tion of the Local Board for sanction to borrow £lO 000 for the purpose of erecting public offices. There were present Messrs. F. H. Pankhurst, T. Handley, B. Dutton, F. Hayes. J. Houghton, J. T. Allen (clerk), F. Holme (architect), and W. Iligginson (surveyor.)—Mr. Allen explained that the site for the proposed new offices was on the ground adjoin- ing the market, and which was acquired some years ago. The tender for the erection of the building was £5,905, but if some extra items were added the arno,pnt would be I£6 937. It was not, however, the intention a the Board tto carry out these additional items at present. Heating ap- paratus, sewering and flagging, and the general finishing off of the interior of the-building, brought up the amount required to £10,( 10. Furnishing was not included, because the furniture in the offices now occupied would supply nearly all the requirements. M. Holme described the plans. The building will be constructed of grey bricks, with terracotta dresangs, and a roof of green elates. Terra cotta is the only material that will resist the corrosive rction of the Widnes atmosphere, and as little stone as possible will be used. On the ground floor are to be the offices of the Local Board, coneisting of the clerk's, the general, the collector's and the nuisance inspector's offices. Conveniently place, will be a strong room arid lavatories. Accommodation for the School Board is also pro- vided on the same floor. In addition to a room for the clerk, a general office, an inspector's office, and a committee room, a waiting room with a separate entrance from the street was shown upon the plans. There is also a strong room fortthe use of the School Board. The caretaker is provided with a living room, a kitchen, and a scullery on the ground floor at the rear of the building, where a fire engine house is also to he erected. On the first floor there is lobe a lofty boardroom, 42 Net by 22 feet, approached by a lobby leading into an anteroom. There are to be two committee rooms, each 16 feet by 15 feet. Upon this floor cmital provision is made for the surveyor. Besides a private office he is to have two drawing offices, and a strong room, and a lavatory. The keeper will alro have a bedroom here, and another at the base of what will be the tower. The grottnd floor is to be coverel with a solid wooden block pavemeut laid in small diagonals upon concrete 6 inches thick, while in the upper storey the flooring will be of pitchpine. The passages will be laid with mosaic flooring, and the whole of the cor- ridor will be fireproof. Questions by the Inspector elicited the fact that it would take quite a year to erect the build- ing, which will stend 15 feet hack from the road. It is exoected that the School Board will pay an annual rent of £7O for their accommodation. The Inspector expressed himself satisfied with the provision shown on the plans, and he was informed that the design of Messrs. F. and G. Holme was chosen from those of 16 or 17 ether competitors. The inquiry then terminated

THE MANCHESTER SITIP CANAL. This Bill on Monday came before Mr. Campion, one of the examiners of the House of Commons, for proof of standing orders after first reading in the Commons. Formal proofs having been given, the Eximioer declared that the standing orders of Parliament had been complied with. Mr. Fester will now in all probability be chairman of , the COMEIIO.I3' Committee on the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, which, it may be expected, will commence its sittings in the second week of next month. The promoters and op- ponents alike are to be congratulated upon this circum- stance, for not only is Mr. Forster known as one of the strongest headed men in the House of Commons, but he is also quite free from having given any expression of opinion upon the Hll, and, while thoroughly acquainted with the wants and feelings of large communities, has no immediate cumection whatever with Lancashire. Mr. Forster's ac- ceptance of this arduous servos is, it is understood, not yet absolute, but it is in a position from which he is not at all likely to withdraw. Two members from the side of the Opposition and one other Ministerialist will form the Committee. At a meeting of the Liverpool City Council, on Welles- ddy, Sir W. B. Forwood said it was import int that the recommendation of the Parliamentary Committee to the effect that the Council oppose the Manchester Ship Canal Bill in the House of Commons, and that the Mayor be 'authorised to affix the common seal to a patition against the bill, should be adopted by the Council in order that the petition might be lodged. A more serious question never affected the interests of the port. If the bar was silted up 31t. it absolutely prohibited large Atlintic liners from entering Liverpool. If the bar were ever silted up one foot they could not measure by any money consideration the terrible resalts that would follow. Toe Ship Canal Bill was the most extraordinary bill ever brought before Parlia- ment, the course pursued by the promoters was the most extraordinary, and it required to be watched day by day and hour by hour by skilled counsel. A motion to pro- secute the opposition to the Canal Bill in the House of Commons, and to engage the same counsel as in the Lords, was unanimously agreed to.

--- ROYALTY AT WARRINGTON.—Yesterday morning the Queen passed through Bank Quay Station, in the Royal train, en route to Bilateral from London. MOVEMENTS OF TROOPS.—Yesterday a detachment of the sth Dragoons halted at Warrington, having left Manchester in the morning, and are expected to leave to-day (Saturday) for their destination, Newb,idge, Ireland. THE IXAMINER, SATiI3JMY. MAY 23, 1885. OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. The negotiations with Russia for the settlement of the Afghan Frontier are still going forward. Yesterday the House of Commons was startled by confirmation of a report current throughout the afternoon that the Guards, home- ward bound from Suakim, had been intercepted and ordered to stay at Alexandria. This is a matter of precaution indi- citing preparation for returning to a warlike attitude should it be necessary. But I believe that it is only a matter of precaution. Ministers who have in their hands all the tbreade if the story do not anticipate a final check to the arrange- ments. The situation is a little difficult for the Conservatives both in the P rem and in Parliament. As soon as the glad tidings of an honourable and satisfactory settlement with Russia were proclaimed, these authorities, avowedly not knowing anythine about it, declared that Mr. Gladstone had surrendered everything to Rotate, had thrown over the Ameer, had flouted the Indian Government, and having done all that was possible in the way of " humiliation " had 80 Obtained a peaceful settlement. They now announce, the I Standard claiming priority for information, that Mr. Gladstone's terms are so high that the Russian Government cannot accept them, and that, therefore, once more war be- comes imminent. I should not be at all surprised, if the negotiations were broken off and war ensued, that Mr. Glad- stone would be condemned for wantonly imperilling peace by demanding from the Czar more than he knew he could concede. The week has been a busy one in Parliament. Business has, in fact, inatead of unduly lagging been pushed for- ward with a haste that is responsible for serious public evil, sad is loudly deplored in the Liberal ranks. By dint of sitting on Wednesday the Lords were able to complete the Registration Bills, having introduced some amendments into the Euglish measure. The alteration, which has led to so much talk, relates to the disfranchisement of voters who ac- cept gratuitous medical relief. Ls Committee in the House of Commons the principle had bees established that a man Iso doing should not therefore be disfranchised. The Lords struck out this clause. They were obliged, with whatever show of cordiality, to admit to the exercise of the franchise an additional two million voters, largely. composed of egri- cultural labourers. But if by any means they could diminish the number, filch away tha vote from a larger or smeller iproportion, it cm hardly be wondered that they jumped at ithe opportunity. Hem they gained it, and it is estimated I that many thousands of the newly enfranchised are by this I stroke disfranchised. The indignation felt on the Liberal benches at this turn of events found expression in the debate on Wednesday. The Attorney-General urged as the only reason for agreeing , , with the Lords' amendments, that if any conflict were Iraised, including the necessity ef returning the Bill to the Lords, the measure might be endangered, it being abso- lutely necessary in order to come into work before the \ General Election that it ehould receive the Royal Assent this week. Member after member rose and protested against this process of legislation, Mr. Firth hotly declaring that lthe lionee of Commons had been "cornered by the Lords." I But everybody knew well enough that in this case the Losotrednstawtieoruesilnynoicevenetlieadndatththeeprotests and reproaches they \ wereis that reallyh t e , directed in another quarter. ilToleuesepolfainLofradcst : reason why this greet wrong has been done is that the ' Queen had arranged to go to Balmoral on Thursday night, ' and no one seems to have had the courage to represent to ' Her Majesty the public advantage that would accrue if she \ ' were to postpone her journey by 24 hours. No one can ' I doubt from what is known of Her Majesty's sense of public I duty that she would not have held for a moment in the balance any personal inconvenience that might have arisen from brief delay of a holiday journey as compared with the electoral rights of a large section of the people. r l As was pointed out by more than one speaker, with a pretty air of being unable to comprehend the situatien, there was no reason in the world, as far as the Lords were con- cerned, why the House of Commons should not have had an opportunity of exercising its privelege, and in truth of doing its simple duty. Whilst the Commons were discus- sing the Lords' amendments in the early hcurs of Wednes- day afternoon, the Lords were iti attendance to deal with the result, whatever it might be. They met at eleven o'clock, passed the bill through its formal stages, and then I " adjourned during pleasure," that is to say, remained ' within call to take up the bill when it should come back from the Commons. They could on Wednesday have de- bated and decided upon the course they should adopt. It might have been that they would have accepted the Com- mons insistence upon this point, and there would have been an end of it. If, on the contrary, they had determined to stand by their own amendments, the Commons at tonight's sitting would have been informed of the fact, a conference might forthwith have been arranged, and the matter settled. But by that time the Queen would have been already on her way to Scotland, and her signature to the Royal Com- mission could have been obtained only in a hasty and in- formal manner, with which her Majesty, who is most punc- tilons on these points, is understood not to approve. Sa the two million electors who were to have been placed on the poll in time for the general election will find their numbers seriously decreased, and the newly enfranchised- disfranchised will have to wait till the new Parliament gets to work in a happier concatenation of circumstances to secure their rights. The great publishing event of the week, with one excep- tion the greatest in history, is the publication of the re- vised edition of the Old Testament. The other was, of course, the issue of the revised edition of the New Testa- ment. The interest excited in the ehtent is strong indica- tion of the hold the Bible has upon the English nation. Many details of this feeling have been given in the daily papers. I happen to have received on Tuesday night a letter, written the same morning by a well-known preacher. Amidst remarks on various matters appears the following sentence :—" I am waiting with strong desire the coming of the New Bible; expected now every minute." It was evi- dent he had sent out early in the morning to purchase the book, and was now sitting in his study impatiently awaiting Its arrival, trying to occupy his thoughts by miscellaneous letter writing,but unable to keep out of the body of his letter a reference to the all-absorbing tbonght. I confess that I felt great apprehension at the possible manner of dealing with the work. There are so many pas- sages the music of which might be marred by a touch that could nevertheless be justified upon the ground of accurate translation. We laugh at the old lady who derived much spiritual benefit from the pronunciation of "that blessed word Mesopotamia." But there are many passages in the unrevised version of the Old Testament which have not any more meaning, and yet which linger noon the memory like the refrain of a sweet familiar tone. For example there is the line in the old book," Canat thou bind the sweet influ- ence of the Pliades ?" That is a perfect line, most musi- cal in its rhythm. But if anyone were asked the meaning in this connection of "binding sweet influences," he would be at a loss for a satisfactory reply. To make a frank con- fession, till I saw the new version it never occurred to me that this line is a little mixed in meaning. The new read- ing," Canst thou bind the cluster of the Pleiades," at once clears up the difficulty, and leaves the line almost as charm. log to the ear. How the old translators dragged in "sweet influences" will now Dever be known. There seems more room for guessing how it came to pass that the still older translators made of the question, "Is there any balm In Gilead?" "Is there any treacle in Gilead?" The work of the revisers is to my mind a much more decided success than the revision of the New Testament. Under the direction of Mr. Henry Frowcie full justice has been done to the new edition in the matter of material form. In all its various issues, cheap, or comparatively costly, the revised version is a triumph of typographical art and binders' work. It is some time since we heard anything of the Claimant. The project of a series of lectures fell through, pertly be- cause the public did not heartily respond to invitations to come and see the great man at so much a head, and partly, it is understood, because a hint was received from the Home Office that as the Claimant was on ticket-of-leave it was not, on the whole, desirable that he should amnia too prominent a public position The most practicable and com- mon-sense proposition was that his friends should set him up in a public-house. But up to the present time this pro- ject has not been viewed with favour by " Sir Roger." I hear from one of the faithful that "Sir Roger" has by no means abandoned his hope of proving his right to the title and estates. There is talk of an indispensable and in( on- trovertable witness who is to set the whole matter right. This person has been discover( I in the piece where many other rich discoveries have been made, namely California. It is even said that a sum of £lOO has been sent out tee the Far West to prosecute the inquiry, aud that a telegram has been received from San Francisco stating that the witness his been discovered, and that his evidence is in every re- spect satisfactory. Nothing better illustrates the tone of Lonionem with re- spect to Mr. Gladstone than the crowd which daily sur- rounds a shop window in St. James'-strcet, where are ex- hibited a succession of cericatures. These are poor in design, defective in drawing, and almost entirely devoid of humour. But they extol Lard Beaconsfield and display Mr. Gladstone in all kinds of humiliating circumstance-. So the crowd looks on and grins and goes its way and mar- vels how a kind Providence can keep in office such a man. The last addition to this gallery represents Mr. Gladstone as being kicked from place by "the wild mob's million feet " of which the poet laureate spoke in his recent dog- grel on the fleet.

Now that the Soudan expedition is definitely abandoned, the Imperial war find and the Princess of Wales's Aid Society will find their occupation gone ; but it is yet to be seen whether the victories of the Canadian troops and the capture of Rid l will similarly do away with the necessity for the effort known by the somewhat coulbersome title of "The Princess Louise's British Fund for the Assistance of the Canadian Troops now serving in the North-West Terri- tories." The ladies' committee of this fund includes not only Princess Louise, as the wife of the immediate ex- Governor-General of the Dominion, and the Dowager Mar- obionelp of Lansdowne, as the mother of the present Gove- nor-General, but a born Canadian who, under the name of " Mrs. E. Albani Gye," will not appear as familiar to most as if her accustomed title of" Mad me Albani" had been niven. According to common report the cognomen " Al- bani " was choF,en as a star-name, because of a prolonged residence at Albany, the official capital of the State of New

going into Committee on the bill. He said that in Committee he should be prepared to give care- ful consideration to any alternative scheme that might be proposed provided it did not inflict on the country greater cost than that which he proposed. He defended the scheme carried out in the bill as the best that could under present circumstances be devised, and said that the objections to it would be found, if it ever came into practice, purely imag- inary.—After observations from Mr. Hibbard, Mr. Ruston, and Mr. Warten, the bill was read a second time. • THE PROTECrION OF GIRLS.-Sir W. HARCOURT moved the second reading of the Criminal Amendment Bill, the object of which was to prevent the traffic in young girls for the purposes of prostitution abroad. The Protection of Girls of Tender Years' Bill, which bad come down from the House of Lords, contained clauses to prevent defilement of girls under fifteen, and he explained that he should not object if the age was raised to 16.—Xr. GIBSON, while supporting the second reading, strongly objected- to clause nine, which, if left in, he felt certain would shipwreck the b ll.—Professor STUART also objcted to some of the clauses.-111r. RASHES said he should move in committee to , raise the age of young women affected by the fifth clause to 16.—After a discussion the motion for the second reading of . the bill was talked out by Mr. C. Bentinck. The House adjourned for the holidays at five minutes to , seven until Thursday, June 4th.

Sir Charles Dilke left London for Dublin on Friday. The health of Mr. Bright, who remains at Llandudno, has much improved. Mr. Gladstone left London by the 4-45 train from Pad- dington on Friday afternoon, for Hawarden. Colonel Stevvart's will, dated Khartoum, March, 1834, a'tested by General Gordon and Frank Pawer, leaves his property an.ong his Irish relatives. A meeting for the examination of B tale George Goldsmid, stockSroker, who abacondel, was adjaurned on Friday, the debtor not haying been beard of. The liabilities are stated at .£30C.000. The Manchester polies made another raid on Friday, selecting the Ellesmere and Prince of Wales, two of the principal sporting clubs in the city. 130 persons were found in the two clubs, but only twelve arrests were made. The tug Granite City returned to Aberdeen on Friday, after a fruitless search for the brig Nordaman of Stavanger, which was seen waterlogged off the coast two days ago. There is little doubt that she has foundered with a crew of about ten men. THREE FISHERMEN DnowNED.lnformation was received at Wick, on Friday, that Angus Coiner and William Bain, local fishermen, together with a hired man, were thrown overboard while passing Cape Wrath, on their way t ) Stor- noway, and drowned. A BANKER COMMITTED FOS ALLEGED FRAIIDS.—At Croydon, en Friday, Augustus Christian, a London mer- chant and banker, was committed for trial on the charge of frauds and forgeries in connection with bills of exchange drawn on Mason, Netzler, and Co ,commission agents, te o years ago.
COUNTY ANTRIM ELECTION. LIBERAL VIC 'CRY. _ . .

The polling in County' A—nt-ri-rn--C-Pened at eight am, on Thursday, at twenty stations. The candidates were Mr. W. P. Sinclair (L.), of Liverpool, and the Hon. R. O'Neill (C.) The weather wan fine, and many vehicles were employed. The polling closed throughout the county at five o'clock. The county is a large one. The ballot boxes were taken to Belfast on Thursday night. On Friday morning the counting of the votes commenced in the County Court- house. Belfast. Great excitement prevailed not only in Belfast, but over the county as to the result of the poll. An immense crowd assembled around the Courthouse pa- tiently awaiting the announcement of the result, which was made as follows :- 1 Sinclair (L) 3,971 O'Neill (C) 3,832
Majority.. ...... 139 Great enthusiasm exists amongst the Liberals of Belfast, and the Conservative party is utterly dumfounded. REPORTED CABINET DIFFERENCES..

a..., —a-a-- A Birmingham correspondent telegraphs : There is con- siderable excitement in Birmingham political circles in con- sequence of the impending resignation of Mr. Chamberlain over the Crimes Act. There have been many inquiries at the Liberal Association offices, but the secretary (Mr. Allard) states that he knows nothing of the political situation be- yond what appears in the newspapers. The Daily News says :—We have reason to believe that a difference of opinion which might have important results has developed itself in the Cabinet on the subject of the partial renewal of the Irish Crimes Act. There is a small but i,,fluential section of the Cabinet which is opposed to the renewal of the Act, unless accompanied by a large measure of local government. The Press Association states that there were again rum- ours in the Parliamentary Lobby on Thursd..y evening that at least one member of the Cabinet might be expected shortly to resign. There is, however, believed to be little or no foundation for these rumours beyond the somewhat , widespread opinion that the Ministry are by no means un- animous on the subject of renewing any provision of the Crimes Act in Ireland, nor with reference to the nature of the contemplated modifications in the Budget proposals.— In the House of Commons the resolution of which Mr. John Morley has given notice against the re-enactment of any portion of the Crimes Act for Ireland is believed to have the sympathy of at least two members of the Cabinet, and is likely to be supported by most of the Ulster Liberal • members, many Radicals, and all Mr. Parnell' Parliamen- tary followers.

THE GUARDS AT ALEXANDRIA. ALEXANDRIA, FRIDAY.—Her Majesty's Indian troopship Jumna arrived here this morning with the greater portion of the Scots and Grenadier Guards. The hired trans- port Deccan, with the remainder of the brigade, is expected to-morrow. DEATH OF VICTOR HUGO. PARIS, FRIDAY.—This morning Victor Hugo still lin- gered, but the doctors have no hopes of his recovery. The Archbishop of Paris offered to attend him, but he declined spiritual aid. It is stated that M. Hugo has bequeathed his manuscripts to the State, and leaves the Government to decide as to his funeral and burial place. Pants, FRIDAY, 2 P.M.—Victor Hugo is dead. The great poet passed away at half-past one. He was born at Besan- con. February 26tu, 1802, his father being a colons' in the French army. ARAB RISING ON THE CONGO.—MASSACRE AND PILLAGE. _ _

The Globe states that-a-rarnaTnTnews has reached Paris from the Upper Congo. Tbe Arabs, excited by the success of the Mandi, have raised an army of 3,000, and are march- ing to conquer the country. On the route they are pillag- ing and massacring, and the natives at different stations of the International Association are flying for their lives. The leader claims the land as the property of the Sultan of Zanzibar. THE SUAKIM RAILWAY MATERIAL. The Press Association understands that owing to the , want of facilities at Suakica Harbour it has been computed that the large fleet of hir( d transports conveying railway material would not be able to land their cargo within six months. A meeting of the chief officials of the War and Admiralty Departments has been held to consider whether it would not be advisable to order the ships toe bring their cargoes away to other ports Or to England, as the amtunt for tonnage which!the Government will have to pay for the delay at Suakim would be almost as much as the railway material is worth. It is believed that the majorits of officials favour bringing the material to England. LORD WOLSELEY. CAIRO, FRIDAY AFfERNOON.—Lord Wolseley has just arrived. His stay has is expected to be short. The Queen arrival at Balmoral at half-past three o'clock oit Friday afternoon.
ENGLAND AND RUSSIA.

A Times second edition telegram, dated Meshel, May 19th, says the Afghan Frontier Mission marched towards Perupa Pass, in the vicinity of Herat, on Monday. The heat is in- creasimr, but the health of the mission is good. Orders have been received at Liverpool for the hasty pre- paration of the transport steamers now in that port, and, in compliance with these instructions, the Dominion Company's steamers Oregon and Vancouver will leave the Mersey immediately. Sir Cooper Key was at Liverpool on Friday inspecting the armed cruisers Orders were received at Sheerness on Friday, directing a draft of seamen to be despatched to Portsmouth for ser- vice in the Cormorant and other vessels preparing for com- mission.
LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four p clock. _

QuEsnoNs.—Mr. Ilisnav, replying to Mr. Broadhurst, admitted that the practics OT stamping advertisements on French copper coin was reprehensible, but there was nothing illegal in so doing —Lord EIMITINGTON, replying to Mr. Bartlett, said be would telegraph to Lord Wolselev to see if anythimg further could be done relative to European prisoners alleged to be in the power of the Mandi.—Mr. CrIADSTONE, replying to Mr. Bartlett, said the Government had no intention of organising an Asiatic or African force, under British officers, to testore order and put down slavery in the Soudan. -

THE EGYPTIAN LOAN.-11,.. GLADsTorrE, replying to gues.tions, stated, as to the satisfaction of the arrangements for a guarantee of the Egyptian Loan, that it had been reported on favourably by the Committee of the French Chambers, and he anticipated that it would be ratified in due course. As to Germany and Austria, the Government had reason to believe that it would be ratified by the close of the summer, the periods of sitting of the respective legislatures. Nothing had occurred to cause the Govern- ment to believe that the delay arose from any objection to the guarantee. SIXPENNY TEurtrams.—On the motion made for the second reading of the Telegraph Acts Amendment Bill, Alderman LAWRENCE urged that a fixed charge of three- pence should be made for addresses of sender and receiver, and expressed a hope that before the full discussion that was to be taken on the motion for the bill going inte Com- mittee, the Government would modify the provisions of the bill.—Mr. PrLESTON contended that the bill was a departure from the resolution of the House that theta should be six- penny telegrams. The plan laid down in the bill was unsatisfactory, bat had the Government given them sixpenny telegrams pure and simple, with free:addresses, the result would have been a profit.— Dr. CAMERON urged the House to accept the bill rather than insist on free addresses, which, if carried, would lead to the withdrawal of the bill.—Alderman COTTON said the refusal of free addresses took away all the good to be de- r;ved from sixpenny tele.-Jams.—Mr. SHAW LEFEVRE looked upon the present debate as merely a rehearsal of that to be raised by Lord John Manners on

RADICALS AND THE CHURCH. Sir,—The Liberationists seem to be wakening up to A. greater sense of their duties. During the last number of months the time of English politicians has been taken up with anxiously watching the alternative moves of England. and Russia, and as there is a slight abatement of the Jingo fever, we may now turn our attention to matters closely in- teresting us at home. The question of Disestablishment has sow become a burning question, and calls loudly for im- mediate settlement. Lord Randolph Churchill recently de- clared that "The Church of England is a great political force on the Tory side." s This is true, and, alike in town and country, "it has," in the words of Mr. Harwood, him- self a great Church supporter, "for the most part been nearly always on the wrong side, on the side of privilege against right, on the side of ignorance against knowledge, on the side of restriction against freedom, on the side of the few against the many." This is a strong indictment, Mr. Editor, but none know better than the supporters of the Establishment how true it is, and I was especially pleased to note in your leaderette of the 16th inst. the few trenchant remarks respecting its most recent doings in Earlestown and Warrington. With Radicals the question of Disestablish- ment is of vital importance ; they view its vast revenues with great concern, knowing as they do, that of all levellers Free Education is the most ommipotent, and in the reven- ues of the State Church, the means to secure it lie ready to their hands. Rev, gentlemen like Mr. Carleton may view this concern of the Radicals as so much dishonesty, may even use very much stronger terms in describing it, but the fact remains that it is only in districts where trade and agriculture flourish and prosper, that the revenues of the Church maintain their required sums. It is quite obvious from this that the revenues of the church are derived directly from the toiling and moiling of the millions. I have before me numbers of cases spreading all over England, wherein those having the cure of souls have been forced to seek other means of gaining a livelihood in consequence Of the great decrease of revenue from lands set aside, and now controlled by the "dead band," for church purposes. I should have no fault to find with the Church. were its revenues derived from voluntary sources, but the £10,000,000 a year it receives represents so much compulsory toil, so many compulsory payments, that it is now high time that the nation put its foot down firmly and insisted upon this state of thiegs being at once ended. A terribly long list of indictments mould be brought against the State Church, but these coming from confessed opponents, would not be half so valuable as the charges brought by its own friends and supporters. I see the Church Defence Association issues a leaflet in which ten reasons are given why the Church should not be disestablished, one of which reads—" You would lose the means of grace which ' you now possess • without money and without price.' This, Mr. Editor, I must characterise as a piece of unblush- ing impudence. Do supporters of the State Church mean to tell the people that this." grace" which they now receive without money and without price " will be withheld so soon as a voluntary system is introduced? Is this not a free and open confession that it is not the souls of the poor that are cared for, but rather the results of their labour ? The passage itself lacks logical sequence. Another passage reads—" You would lose God's ministers to baptize your children, to marry your sons and daughters, and to bury your dead." This passage, for baseness, is unrivalled by any in the list, and I should very much like some of your readers to make it clear. In the event of disestablishment, would those who are now "God's ministers" become the devil's? or weuld they leave the Church and seek secular employment? If the latter event phould happen it would be a bad job for the people, for, as incapacity is their char- acteristic in the pulpit, what would it be in the mills or counting houses? And respecting the baptism of children, the Baptists get on very well without it, and seem none the worse off, and the Legislature has declared marriage to be a civil rite, so that our sons and daughters need not tremble. It is the unblushing arrogance of the Church party in claiming "Church clubs and charities,' "Church funds for the sick and needy," " Church schools for the education of the children." It is asserted that all this will be lost when the Church is disestablished. In this the Church party ap- peal, as they have ever done, to the base and sordid side of human nature. They distrust the people, and yet what sup- port do they get from the people in the shape of church attendance ? Literally none; churches exist for the aris- tocracy and the middle classes. Sir,—lf you have any regard for the feelings of your readers never print such a report again. Your own good senseyught to have put a scotch upon such scurfy transac• (ions. Talk about infeztion ! You have no idea of the sensation it has caused amongst your readers. lam not one of the moat sensitive of mortals, but sinca reaiing the report I have had an inclination to rub against every lamp- post that I have come near, and the result in one case has been of a very serious character. Mr. Appleton sent home a boy's suit in a paper containinz the report, and the lad has itched ever fence. For this I hold you responsible ; you really must exercise more care in what you admit into your paper, if you intend to keep up its respect- ability. The ratepayers of the Union have spent a large amount of money to remove the children from the imaginary taint of pauperism. But " Great Scot !" if the choice has to be made betwixt pauperism and the itch, by all that's noble give me honest pauperism. The people of rie Warrington Union up to now have flattered themselves th....t in securing the services of Mr. Darbyshire they had got a model chair- man. Oh fle ! Mr. D., is that the way you look after the 'brats ?" After the disclauree that- have been made, can yeti ever look an honest woman in the face again? It was time for you to retire, but what abut the honours? The School Committee are not composed to my liking. To understand children a man must have had a baby of his own. I respect Mr. Hunt, but he kaows nothing about "cinder tea," and never saw a baby, except at arm's length. If all men were to wrap up their talents in a napkin as he has done, Padgate Schools would soon be in the market. The Guardians are to blame. The School Committee ought to be cemposed of family men. Dr. Mackie and Mr. Bal. harry would be a wise selection. How the nurses have escaped the contagion is" a thing no fellow can understand." Mr. Mine's "luxuriant health " must be very dangerous to him, yet if there is one in the whole establishment that de- serves an itching sensation it is Mr. Mines. I should just like to see him have it for a month. Wouldn't Pad- gate be fumigated! Dr. Spinks says he has got a lotion that will cure the itch by two applications. It this Is true, Warrington is no place for Dr. Spinks • " a-yont the Tweed" his fortune is made, and Dr. Hornb'rook is cast in the shade. In conclusien. Mr. Editor, let me say that I always con- sidered that in the Padgata Schools the Guardians had got a white elephant. but I never expected it to turn out a scabby one.--Yours truly, BUNK KAY. Earlestown, May 21st, 1885.

MR. BRADLAUGH'S VISIT. Sir,—l think that those who have been instrumental in bringing our modern " iconoclast " to Warrington are break- ing the ice in a very useful direction. The privilege of supply- ing the political pabulum of the people of Warrington has too much been left in the hands of the two orthodox par- ties. The efforts of these parties, and particularly of the party which advocates progress and improvement, are, no I doubt, right enough in their way, but we all know that poll- -11 Beal sects, like religious sects, are very much addicted to setting up arbitrary standards of faith, and to branding those I who do not conform to these standards as "heretics." They are always striving to make people not only "vote square but also to think square, and tne political aliment they provide is generally carefully prepared to further this end. But political questions have.more than two sides, and an address by a comparatively independent man like Mr. Bradlaugh generally brings things into view which were not generally thought about. It does, however, seem a pity that they did not time his visit a day later. They would thus have made a happy precedent; for, I should think, no other place in England of anything like its size is pro- vided with so few means of passing a Sunday in a rational and useful way as this town. If a man does not care for the Dead Sea fruit of theology which is ministered out with an automston-like uniformity in chapels on Sunday, or if he feels a natural and manly repugnance to being enrolled in tke emasculated army of Sunday school teachers, what is he to do on the Sundays? The truth is, to quote the words of the pathetic street song, he has "got nothing to do." This state of affairs would be to a great extent changed w,ra a series of Sunday lectures on instructive themes to be arranged, and therefore I regret that the occasion of Mr. Bradlaugh's visit has not been used to break the ice in this direction also. JAQUES.

am not astonished to -re-a-ci-in your paper the dis- closures made by Mr. Henley at the Workhouse Schools, but before the public say "Amen" to his severe striAures allow one who knows scmething of workhouse and hospital I management to say a word in palliation of the position of the officials, and the treatment they receive at the bands of the collective wisdom of the Board. Take the medical officer first, who, whatever bin faults may be, has grown grey in their service. How often during the last 30 years has Mr. Spinks made recommendations which have been ignored ; and this constant inattention to his wishes may have made him feel that time after time similar entries have been made with no avail. Members of the Board of 10 or 20 years' standing know perfectly well that the itch is a standing dish at the work- house. Why have they waited for Mr. Henley to say it can be stamped out like any other contagious disease? The fact is there are too many masters in connection with Pauper Authority. Appoint good officials, and let the Board of Management give them their confidence, and when any- thing of an unsatisfactory' character art es, lot it first be dealt with in camera, and then, if not remedied, make it public, or discharge the officer. But, as at prerent, you have evils in existence which will require for their elimination a cemplete reform—from the present political election of the Board, down to the appointment of the porter at the gate.— Yours, AN EX-GUARDIAN.
THE IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE. Bir,—ln justice I think you ought to allow me a short space in your newspaper in reply to I‘ll. " Clifford Dix's " . .
two letters which, in my opinion, have shown a vast amount _ _

of El-feeling against the; cause Which all..Mv-er's-OfTWri-2-7 ad justice have at heart. In perusing his amusing and ridiculous letters I find there is no sound good meaning of any kind in them ; nothing but a tirade against Ireland and ' Irishmen. It appears Mr. Dix doesn't or won't read much about Irish history or he would know how that noble coun-

try has been trodden upon from time to time by various bad Governments. The National League meeting held in this town was presided over by a worthy and esteemed Irish- man, of whom every Irishman in Warrington ought to be proud for doing his duty in the cause which all Irishmen I have at hegrt, namely. Home Rule for Ireland with the

same gracious good Queen, Lords and Commons to rule over us. But power to be given to Ireland to manage hr internal affairs the same as the late Isaac Butt, wanted, and yet to be under the B itish Empire. There is nothing would give the Irish people satisfaction but a fair . . " " " '• .

trial, the same as Canada, AuStralia ; and ir is time to ask the British Parliament for Horne Rule through Ireland's gallant leader, Charles Stewart Parnell, M.P. Talk of Cromwell's extermination! Ireland has lost within the last 10 years more of her population, more of her life-blood, than the whole population of the country amounted to in the time of Oliver Cromwell. They have been extermina- ted wholesale from the land of their birth by cruel and bad landlords. They have filled workhouses first, jails next, and then the emigrant ships, filled with Ireland's sons and daughters, driven like a flock of sheep to make way for some foreign adventurer—taking the homes from over the Irish people's beads, some of them not owing one penny, to make the good pasture of Ireland fit for nothing, and keep at their disposel game and deer. "Clifford Dix" says that the Irish portion of our fellow- townsmen should not suppose that the Liberal party are oppcsed to agitation carried on in a coastithtional manner. The Irish people of this borough know their sad grievances better than 100 such men as Mr. Dix can tell them. Net by his windy eloquence or hie false statements will the Irish- men of Warrington be hoodwinked, bat follow their noble leaders. As regards Mr. Biggar's speech, it is one that the Irishmen of Warrington are not responsible for, bat at the same time the gallant member has done his duty to the Irish Parliamentary party, which all Irishmen should be proud of. Mr. Dix next attacks Mr. Cox, and says that be had the benefit of listening to his speech. I must assert, said Mr. Dix, titat under no Government would such a speech be alowed. I can tell Mr. Dix that no country where truth and justice are interfered with will prosper. He boasts of the freedom of the Press, which all Radicals uphold, and still be wants to gag Mr. Cox, not only by his presence at the meeting, but by his simple and amusing letters. Why did Mr. Dix keep away from the meeting last Sunday, when he would have had the presence and comfort of hearing from Mr. Cox an excellent speech about Ireland's past and present ? He next mikes false charges against the officers of the Irish National League. I tell Mr. Dix and the public that some of the clergymen of Warrington could not attend the meeting through religious duties, er they would have been present ' • nevertheless, they sent letters of apology. What right has Mr. Dix to melee such random ettteinents when I tell him plainly, after livin some 30 years in this prosperous two, that he knows nothing about dictating to us what we will do at the coming parliamentary election. Now, sir, as there are two sides to a question, with your permission I will give Mr. Dix some few correct figures for the much-needed Home Rule for Ireland. I find that in past [years there has been drained out of Irelend by absentee land- lords rents, revenue, and customs alone (from 1800 to 1810) £7,500,000 yearly, customs and revenue £5.000,000 yearly The total loss from 1800 to 1876 at c nn- pound interest is £7,895,000,000. What remedy would Mr. Dix ask of the Government to cure this enormous amount of money 1 laving Ireland? In my simple opinion nothing will cure it but Home Rule, or some better form of good government, not by gagging the people, but by compelling some of the runaway landlords te spend a fair proportion of the money they receive from the poor peasantry upon the industry of Ireland and her people. The British Government sees daily 5,00,000 men and women crying for bread; poverty stricken on the soil of Ireland. It may be covered with soldiers from Dublin to Galway. and from Cork to Londonderry, but that will not do any longer without some local good measures are adop- ted to stop the tide of Irish emigration.—Yours. PHILIP O'BRIEN.

The advertising columns of the London newspapers con- tain the usual announcements of train excursions for Whit- suntide, and, as is customary, a special feature is made of the various city offices at which tickets can be procured in advance. One wonders if it ever occurs to such inteasely conservative bodies as railway boards generally are, that Ibis system is capable of inflate expansion, and that, if it were expanded, the resu't could scarcely fail to be pecuni- arily benedcial to themselves. If it were possible to pro- cure, not at half -a-dez 3n, but at a couple of score of offices or shops in various parts of the metropolis, tickets in ad- vance for long railway journeys, one of the nuisances now attendant upon travelling could be avoided.

• GEORGE SHEFFIELD. (LINES FOR AN ALBUM.) George Sheffield's a -wonderful man— A wonderful artist is he ; With his seeing eye and his cunning hand, He will make you a picture of sea or of land— Of ship, or tower, or tree. He's at home on the roaring main, When the loud winds lash the deep ; He will paint you this, and then, again, He will shoWyou the sea one great, smooth plain As calm as a child asleep. It is now a country scene— A river glowing and bright, With clumps of trees and a church bet +nen ; It is now a tale of what has been— A castle stormed in the night. In colour, or "black and *site," He has ever a marvellous touch ; I've seen him lay " soot " on as black as night, And instantly turn it to clear moonlight— He once made a picture with " slutch." He's a comet amongst his kind— A spurner of bolts and bars, And if ever he leaves this earth behind, You will find he has mounted the wings of the wind To go painting amid the stars. ED. Ex. Warrington, May 22nd, 1885.
